articles.title: Egypt approves military support for Saudi Arabia against Houthis
articles.summary: Egypt’s parliament authorized Monday military support for Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi attacks, following a request from President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi. The House of Repr...
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s parliament authorized Monday military support for Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi attacks, following a request from President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi.
The House of Representatives "approved authorizing President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," state newspaper Al-Ahram reported.
The parliament, stacked with supporters of el-Sissi, had held three rare secret meetings on the matter and postponed the vote twice.
The president last week had asked parliament to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, "if requested."
It was not immediately clear what defensive support could be provided by Egypt, the Arab world's largest military, which boasts hundreds of thousands of active personnel, fighter jets and complex air defenses sourced from countries including the U.S., China, France and Russia.
El-Sissi said Wednesday that his country's support would be to "defend Saudi territory and does not include an attack on Yemen."
"We are talking about defending the land and borders of the kingdom," he said in a speech, adding that the top priority was for a diplomatic solution.
Egypt has undertaken a flurry of diplomatic maneuvers since, with Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty consulting with the so-called R4, which includes members of the Mecca defense pact, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, which Cairo has not agreed to join.
On Monday, he said he was "talking daily with the Iranians" to push for regional de-escalation.

articles.title: From the Mecca defence pact to Tehran talks: Is the Middle East’s security landscape shifting? - Euronews.com
articles.summary: From the Mecca defence pact to Tehran talks: Is the Middle East’s security landscape shifting?  Euronews.comSaudi defence pact countries push for peace in Tehran as Houthis launch more attacks  ReutersFlurry of Diplomacy in Iran Amid Reports of U.S. and Israeli Plans to Renew War  The New York TimesOil ticks lower as Saudi defense minister meets with Iran's president in Tehran to de-escalate  CNBCMecca defence alliance members in Tehran to defuse Iran-US, ...
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are pursuing talks with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of the Mecca Defence Alliance.
Senior military and security officials from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are holding talks with Iranian officials in Tehran as diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Iran and the United States continue.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey are members of the Mecca Defence Alliance, a security alliance established amid regional instability and concerns over threats linked to Iran and its allies.
The three countries have now turned to direct talks with Tehran about regional security, even as the alliance faces growing pressure from attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin are attending the talks in Tehran on Monday, according to Saudi and Iranian officials.
They are reportedly meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has described the meeting as a potential step towards establishing cooperative regional security mechanisms.
Speaking at his weekly news conference in Tehran, Baghaei reiterated Iran’s longstanding call for what it describes as "endogenous security," a framework that would rely primarily on the capabilities and interests of regional countries.
The Mecca pact: collective defence against regional threats
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August 2026. Under the pact, an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all three, requiring the others to provide assistance.
The agreement brings together Saudi Arabia’s financial resources and influence in global energy markets, Pakistan’s nuclear capabilities and Turkey’s advanced defence industry and NATO membership.
Although the agreement was signed amid growing concerns over Iran and its allied groups, Turkish officials have insisted that it is not directed against Tehran or any other specific country.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in an Aug. 8 interview with Anadolu that the agreement did not identify any country as a common threat. He explained that countries would not be considered targets unless they attacked a signatory.
The agreement has received approval in Pakistan, while Turkey has submitted it to parliament but has yet to complete the ratification process.
Houthi attacks put collective defence to the test
Escalating missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi Arabia have presented the Mecca alliance with its first major test.
At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the three countries agreed to move towards implementing their collective defence commitments, including measures to ensure the rapid deployment of agreed military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia.
The commitments were outlined in a joint statement published by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry.
Ankara, however, has drawn a line between supporting Saudi Arabia’s defences and joining offensive military operations against the Houthis inside Yemen.
At an Oct. 8 news conference in Ankara, Fidan said the agreement was defensive and ruled out sending Turkish troops to another country to carry out attacks.
Turkey has instead been assessing possible contributions in areas such as air defence, electronic warfare and technical assistance.
The three nations are therefore pursuing direct engagement with Tehran while strengthening their military readiness under the terms of an alliance designed to deter attacks on its members.
Why engage with Tehran?
Pakistan has played a mediating role between Tehran and Washington in recent months. Saudi Arabia is seeking to contain the threat posed by Houthi attacks on its territory and infrastructure, while Turkey has sought to prevent further regional escalation.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said in an Oct. 26 post on X that the Tehran visit was part of continued efforts by the Mecca pact countries to reduce tensions and encourage diplomatic solutions.
He said the talks were also intended to support mediation efforts by Qatar and Pakistan.
The Saudi statement suggests that talks with Iran are being pursued alongside the alliance’s defence commitments, rather than necessarily representing a fundamental change in the pact’s purpose.
Military deterrence or regional security?
Tehran’s emphasis on locally driven security arrangements appears, at least in principle, to share some common ground with the Mecca pact’s stated objective of strengthening security cooperation among regional states.
Significant differences remain, however.
Saudi Arabia maintains extensive security ties with the United States, Turkey is a NATO member, and Pakistan continues to pursue defence partnerships with several major powers.
Meanwhile, no agreement on a new joint regional security mechanism has been announced.
Nevertheless, the Tehran meeting highlights a notable development: Three countries that have established a mutual defence alliance in response to mounting regional security threats are now also pursuing direct dialogue with Iran.
The key question is whether this dual approach can have a lasting impact on regional tensions.

articles.title: Iran, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan call for regional-led security
articles.summary: Iran said Monday it had reached an understanding with Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that regional security should be maintained by countries in the region rather than foreign...
articles.full_text:
Iran said Monday it had reached an understanding with Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that regional security should be maintained by countries in the region rather than foreign powers, following high-level talks in Tehran focused on strengthening cooperation and addressing shared security challenges.
Iran and three other countries participating in the Mecca pact — Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan — agreed that regional security should be ensured without foreign intervention, a senior Iranian official said Monday.
"The outcomes we agreed on were that security in the region where we live should be endogenous, meaning it should be achieved by the countries themselves, and that we must prevent any kind of foreign intervention in this region," Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said following the meeting.
The four-way talks in Tehran brought together senior officials to discuss regional security, Israel's activities in the Middle East and developments in Palestine and Lebanon.
Türkiye was represented by National Intelligence Organization (MIT) Director Ibrahim Kalın, Saudi Arabia by Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Pakistan by army chief Asim Munir.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also attended the meeting.
Earlier Monday, Pezeshkian expressed Tehran's readiness to deepen regional cooperation and resolve disputes, calling for greater unity among Muslim-majority countries, according to state news agency IRNA.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran, with firm conviction and serious determination, is ready to take steps toward deepening regional cooperation, resolving differences and drawing on the shared capabilities of Islamic countries," Pezeshkian said.
He emphasized that Tehran supported initiatives aimed at promoting regional solidarity, stability and economic development.
The Iranian president also said Muslim countries could harness their collective resources and capabilities to present a model of justice and development to the international community.
The meeting underscored efforts by the four countries to strengthen regional coordination amid continuing tensions in the Middle East.

articles.title: From six-day victory to wars of attrition: How has Israel ended its wars? - Iran International
articles.summary: From six-day victory to wars of attrition: How has Israel ended its wars?  Iran International
articles.full_text:
The current war with Iran raises a question Israel has repeatedly faced: can battlefield gains produce a lasting end to conflict? The Jewish State's military history offers varied answers: victories that left underlying disputes unresolved, withdrawals without formal surrender, and ceasefires that left adversaries armed.
Destroying Iran’s military capabilities and preventing their reconstruction are different objectives, requiring different measures of success.
Since 1948, Israel has fought conventional Arab armies and armed organizations such as Hezbollah and Hamas, and has increasingly confronted Iran directly through missile, drone and air attacks far beyond its borders. These forms of warfare have overlapped, posing different challenges for bringing the fighting to an end.
Their endings show how battlefield outcomes interact with diplomacy, outside pressure and arrangements for security after the fighting.

articles.title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election - The Guardian
articles.summary: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election  The GuardianNetanyahu Pushed for Attack on Iran Ahead of Israeli Election, Officials Say  The New York TimesNetanyahu says U.S. and Israel must topple Iranian regime  The Washington PostReport: Zamir the only security chief to oppose pre-election military action against Iran  The Times of IsraelNetanyahu Goes Into Full Panic Mode  The Atlantic
articles.full_text:
Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.
“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.
In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.
Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.
The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.
As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”
He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.
The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.
The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.
In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”
The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.
In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.
“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”
Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.
His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.
Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

articles.summary: Riyadh airport resumes flights after deadly Houthi attack  Yeni Şafak English
articles.full_text:
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh resumed limited flight operations on Sunday after a roughly two-week suspension caused by a deadly Houthi attack, though the Yemeni group immediately warned that the facility remains a military target and threatened further strikes.
King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh resumed limited flight operations on Sunday after a suspension lasting roughly two weeks, state media reported, though only two terminals reopened and full capacity remains unavailable.
Partial reopening
Terminal 1 resumed domestic flights while Terminal 2 reopened for international services operated by Saudi carriers, AlEkhbariya television reported. The resumption followed intensive coordination between aviation authorities and security agencies to ensure compliance with safety standards, the state-run broadcaster said, while airport management urged passengers to contact airlines before traveling, according to Al Arabiya.
Persistent threats
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the airport "is unsafe because it is a military target for our forces," and pledged continued operations against the facility. Saudi authorities bear responsibility for reopening the airport and any consequences, he added.
Flight operations were suspended after an Oct. 10 Houthi attack killed 13 people and injured more than 300. The Iran-backed group, which controls Yemen's capital Sanaa, resumed fighting Saudi-backed forces in July following the collapse of a 2022 truce.

articles.title: [不同来源] Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile facilities, and other Mideast news - Santa Cruz Sentinel
articles.summary: Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile facilities, and other Mideast news  Santa Cruz Sentinel
articles.full_text:
By The Associated Press
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthi rebels said Monday that it has degraded their ability to strike targets inside the kingdom after destroying tunnels used to store ballistic missiles and missile launchers.
In Israel, the country’s defense minister strongly denied that the military has clashed with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his reported instructions for an “action” against Iran ahead of national elections on Tuesday.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile launchers
An operation in Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and another missile storage facility, according to the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis.
Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said the operation also aimed to cut the Houthis’ supply lines between areas under their control and targeted rebel fortifications and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen.
In a post on X, al-Malki said the coalition would continue to use “deterrent operational measures” to protect against the Houthis’ “brutal attacks” inside the kingdom and in Yemen.
Houthis say Saudi-backed forces struck hospital in Red Sea port city
Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry said Monday that Saudi-backed forces targeted a hospital in the Red Sea port city of Mokha, which the Houthi rebels recently seized. It did not provide evidence for the claim, and The Associated Press could not independently verify it.
In a statement, the ministry said the attack caused extensive damage to the hospital, but did not say whether there were any casualties. It also said Saudi forces on Sunday targeted a children’s hospital in Taiz province, causing damage.
Earlier on Monday, two residents of Mokha, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals, said Mokha General Hospital and at least 10 houses were damaged after a rocket struck a nearby four-story residential building. The AP could not independently verify the claim, and it was not clear if this was the same incident that the Health Ministry was referring to.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-backed forces.
— By Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen
Houthis say they fired missiles at Yemeni government forces
The Houthi rebels claimed Monday that they struck military gatherings and weapons depots belonging to Saudi-backed government forces in Aden and Lahj provinces.
The Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the rebels fired ballistic missiles at the sites, inflicting losses. The claims could not be independently verified.
The Houthis continue to target government forces and their allies inside Yemen. The Yemeni government accused the rebels on Sunday of targeting displacement camps on the outskirts of the southern port city of Aden. The government didn’t provide evidence to support its claim.
Israel’s defense minister denies clash with the army over Iran
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Monday dismissed reports regarding rifts between the political leadership and the Israeli military over Iran as “completely baseless and false.”
In a post on X, Katz also said Israel had no intention to strike Iran before Tuesday’s national elections but that it would respond “with great force” if Iran attacks first.
Israeli Channel 12 reported Sunday evening that Benjamin Netanyahu and Israel’s military chief of staff clashed over the Israeli prime minister’s instruction to carry out an “action” that the army believes could quickly reignite the conflict with Iran. The report did not specify the nature of the action. Netanyahu’s office later described the report as “fake news.”
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan seek closer cooperation
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed Monday to continue talks on strengthening cooperation, particularly on regional peace and security, Iran’s state-run news agency IRNA reported.
Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, hosted the four countries’ first quadrilateral meeting in Tehran.
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s armed forces chief Gen. Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin attended.
The IRNA report did not specify when or where the next meeting would take place.
Meanwhile, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said renewed attacks on Iran would destabilize the region and hurt countries that are not party to the conflict. In a televised address on Monday, he said reports about potential attacks had already driven fuel prices higher.
UN chief ‘alarmed’ by Israeli settler violence
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said Monday he was “deeply alarmed” by surging Israeli settler violence and settlement expansion in the West Bank.
Speaking in Cairo on one of his final trips as U.N. chief, Guterres called for lifting Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid to Gaza and removing obstacles to the Security Council’s peace plan, warning that “the specter of ethnic cleansing” was looming ever larger.
He said lasting peace in the region depends on Palestinians’ right to self-determination and that a two-state solution, with Jerusalem as the capital of both states, is the only viable path.
Guterres also called for restoring stability around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz and ensuring safety around Yemen’s Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Egypt’s parliament approves help to Saudi Arabia
Egyptian lawmakers on Monday approved President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi’s request to support Saudi Arabia in countering Houthi attacks.
The decision comes amid growing public concern that Egypt could become involved in Yemen’s long-running conflict.
Egypt’s highest security body had pledged to provide “all necessary and possible forms of support” to Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity, and safeguard Islamic holy sites.

articles.title: Pakistan, Qatar explore new avenues for trade, investment cooperation - Dawn
articles.summary: Pakistan, Qatar explore new avenues for trade, investment cooperation  Dawn
articles.full_text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan and Qatar have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral economic ties, exploring new avenues for trade and investment, and expanding cooperation across key sectors, including agriculture, food security, manufacturing, information technology, maritime transport and infrastructure.
The commitment was expressed during the second meeting of the Pakistan-Qatar Joint Task Force (JTF) on Trade and Investment, co-chaired by Federal Minister for Commerce Jam Kamal Khan and Qatar’s Minister of State for Foreign Trade Affairs Dr Ahmad bin Mohammed Al-Sayed in Doha.
The meeting reviewed progress in bilateral economic cooperation since the inaugural session in April 2026 and explored practical measures to enhance trade, facilitate investment and develop industrial partnerships between the two countries.
According to a press release issued here on Sunday, representatives of relevant Pakistani ministries participated virtually, while the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC), which serves as the secretariat of the Joint Task Force, coordinated the proceedings from Pakistan.
  Doha’s investment sought in modern agriculture, grain storage facilities and advanced farming technologies
GCC Free Trade Agreement
During the discussions, Pakistan emphasised the importance of an early signing of the Pakistan-Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Free Trade Agreement, seeking Qatar’s continued support in completing the remaining formalities.
The Pakistani side informed the meeting that it had completed its domestic approval process and forwarded the approved agreement text to the GCC Secretariat on Dec 31, 2025.
The proposed agreement is expected to provide a framework for strengthening trade relations and expanding market access between Pakistan and GCC member states.
Pakistan also raised the issue of restrictions on its bone-in meat exports to Qatar and called for an early resolution. It highlighted that a comprehensive technical dossier addressing animal health and food safety requirements had already been shared with the relevant Qatari authorities.
Agriculture and food security featured prominently on the agenda, with Pakistan highlighting a proposed MoU between the Trading Corporation of Pakistan and Qatar’s Hassad Food for rice supply.
The proposal has been submitted to the federal cabinet for approval.
Pakistan invited Qatari investors to explore opportunities in modern agriculture, grain storage facilities, silos, cold storage, integrated cold-chain infrastructure and advanced farming technologies.
Both sides also discussed sustainable food supply arrangements.
Besides, the Pakistani delegation presented investment opportunities in the automobile sector, particularly electric vehicles under the country’s new EV policy framework.
Joint manufacturing, technology transfer and industrial partnerships were identified as areas offering scope for closer collaboration.
Pakistan also invited Qatari investment in IT and digital infrastructure, shipping and maritime transport.
The proposed Karachi-Hyderabad Motorway was offered as a potential investment opportunity for Qatar.
The Qatari side stressed the importance of enhanced cooperation in civil aviation and air traffic. Pakistan welcomed the proposal and said aviation-related matters would also be taken up by the Technical Working Group on Logistics and Communications.
Investment Fund
Pakistan further presented the concept of an Investment Fund, highlighting opportunities for Qatari participation in infrastructure, agriculture, industrial development, information technology and other priority sectors.
To translate the discussions into practical outcomes, Pakistan called for the early operationalisation of 11 Technical Working Groups identified during the first Joint Task Force meeting. These groups cover logistics, aviation, advanced manufacturing, mining and minerals, agriculture, tourism, financial technology, healthcare, education, industrial development, information technology and startups.
Both countries reaffirmed their commitment to sustained engagement and effective follow-up through the Joint Task Force framework.
Published in Dawn, October 26th, 2026

articles.title: Israeli cease-fire violations kill 7-year-old girl, 3 others across Gaza
articles.summary: Israeli military and Israel-backed gunmen in the Gaza Strip killed four Palestinians, including a 7-year-old girl, and injured 14 others Monday, a medical source said, amid ongoing...
articles.full_text:
Israeli military and Israel-backed gunmen in the Gaza Strip killed four Palestinians, including a 7-year-old girl, and injured 14 others Monday, a medical source said, amid ongoing violations of last year's cease-fire.
The source at Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza told Türkiye's Anadolu Agency (AA) that the bodies of two young men and a girl were brought to the hospital following an airstrike and gunfire in the Bir 19 area west of Khan Younis.
An Israeli drone carried out several strikes on Bir 19, an area housing tents for displaced Palestinians, killing a young man and moderately injuring four others, witnesses said.
Israeli military vehicles also opened heavy fire toward the displacement tents as Israeli-backed gunmen fired in the surrounding area, killing another young man and a 7-year-old girl, who was shot while inside her tent, they added.
Another Palestinian man was killed and four others were injured in an Israeli strike west of Khan Younis, the source said.
Local sources said an Israeli drone struck a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians in the al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis.
Israeli artillery also shelled areas east of Khan Younis as military vehicles stationed east of the city opened heavy fire.
In central Gaza, a Palestinian woman sustained moderate injuries from Israeli gunfire in the Ard al-Shawa area east of Deir al-Balah, another medical source said.
Israeli military vehicles made a limited advance east of Deir al-Balah amid heavy gunfire, witnesses said.
In northern Gaza, Israeli artillery shelled eastern Gaza City as tanks positioned behind the "Yellow Line" opened fire east of the Shujaiya and Tuffah neighborhoods, they added.
The "Yellow Line" marks the area to which Israeli forces withdrew during the first phase of the cease-fire agreement and separates territory under Israeli military control from areas where Palestinians are permitted to remain.
Despite the cease-fire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, the Israeli army has continued daily attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,551 Palestinians and injuring 5,573 others, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others in Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave's civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

articles.summary: Israel continues to commit genocide in Gaza despite a cease-fire agreement, independent U.N.-commissioned experts said in a report Monday, also accusing Israeli forces of crimes ag...
articles.full_text:
Israel continues to commit genocide in Gaza despite a cease-fire agreement, independent U.N.-commissioned experts said in a report Monday, also accusing Israeli forces of crimes against humanity, including torture and rape, in the occupied West Bank.
The Associated Press could not independently corroborate multiple graphic accounts described in the report of sexual assaults by prison guards and soldiers on Palestinian detainees since October 2023. In one, female guards strip-searched a pregnant Palestinian, touching inside her anus and vagina. In another, guards beat a detainee and hurled sexist slurs while denying her access to the toilet and sanitary pads. She bled onto her clothes and interrogation chair.
The findings by the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which seeks to document in minute detail the allegations and evidence of crimes to bolster accountability for perpetrators, could be used by prosecutors at the International Criminal Court or in other jurisdictions to try to bring justice to victims and their relatives.
The report Monday said Israel was "continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”
Much of the harm has come from Israel’s occupation deeper into Gaza during the cease-fire period, the report says. Since October 2025, when the cease-fire was signed, Israeli forces have gone from controlling 53% of Gaza to at least 60%, the commission said.
In that time, Israeli fire across the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians - including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
The report also accused Israeli soldiers and prison guards of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence and persecution against civilians.
The commission said that it had recently documented six cases where Israeli guards were sexually violent toward male detainees from Gaza in the Sde Teiman military prison.
In one case, it says guards raped a Palestinian detainee with a stick, then forced him to put the stick in his mouth until he vomited. It also recalled another episode in which guards instructed a Palestinian man to urinate as they tied a plastic cord around his genitals.
The cease-fire scaled down a devastating war started by the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Israel responded with a genocidal campaign that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

As Israel votes in a pivotal election Tuesday, political analysts and regional policymakers caution that no matter who emerges victorious, the country’s core policies toward the Palestinians, Iran and its position within Middle East are unlikely to experience any significant change.
With polls showing a close contest between incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, both figures are campaigning on hard-line security platforms and share a host of strategic priorities – most notably, maintaining military pressure on Iran and denying Palestinian statehood.
That consensus, analysts argue, stems at least in part from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion and the Israeli genocidal war it triggered, while neighboring Lebanon and Iran became increasingly embroiled on the periphery.
"If Netanyahu is elected, he'll do whatever he thinks he wants to do," said Aviv Bushinsky, a former adviser to Netanyahu. "Expansion of the settlements will continue. The wars against Iran, Hamas and Hezbollah will continue. What you see now is what you'll see after the election, maybe even more aggressively. As long as Iran is in such a situation, it's a waste of time talking about Palestine."
In Bushinsky’s view, echoed by many in Israel’s security establishment and its political class, the electoral contest is less about opposing visions for Israel’s future and more about how far and how fast to push longstanding priorities: confronting Iran, deepening control over the West Bank, and maintaining military deterrence.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot – a former military chief now leading the centrist Yashar party – have publicly opposed the establishment of an independent Palestinian state, a stance now shared by nearly all major Jewish-led parties.
This shift away from the internationally backed "two-state solution” has defined the rightward tilt in Israeli politics. "The substance of the policy remains the same: No to a Palestinian state and yes to further settlement expansion. On this, they are all in agreement," said Palestinian analyst Ghassan al-Khatib.
The West Bank, occupied by Israel since the 1967 Middle East War, has seen a rapid expansion of Israeli settlements under Netanyahu. Critics argue that the government has overlooked or outright enabled increasing violence by terrorist Israeli settlers against Palestinians, as hundreds of thousands of settlers have established themselves in the territory.
While Eisenkot, in contrast, favors settlement "in principle,” he calls for compliance with Israeli law and says that settlements built without official authorization should be dismantled. He has pledged to curb settler violence and opposes building in the contested E1 area of the West Bank, which, if developed, would cut the West Bank in two and sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the territory – an outcome seen by many as the death knell for Palestinian statehood aspirations.
Despite these stylistic differences, Eisenkot supports the continuation of Israeli security control "from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea.” The only notable exception among mainstream parties are the Democrats, the reconstituted center-left faction – and even they appear diminished as the center of political gravity has moved right.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out forming a government with Palestinian-led Israeli parties, which represent about a fifth of the population, foreshadowing the unlikelihood of significant policy reform from any new coalition.
Three years into Israel’s genocidal and a year after a U.S.-brokered cease-fire, Israeli troops now control roughly two-thirds of Gaza, while an estimated 2 million Palestinians remain crowded into the remaining third of the strip. Most live amid the ruins of previous fighting – displaced, under siege, and with little prospect for reconstruction.
Both leading candidates say Israeli forces will remain in Gaza until Hamas is stripped of its weapons and political power, with Eisenkot pledging to replace Hamas’ rule within 18 months, either by international agreement or force of arms. Attempts at negotiating a handover to the Palestinian Authority or a third party have so far failed.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu say Israeli troops will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is disarmed, and that Israel is prepared to restart fighting to achieve this, according to a Reuters analysis.
Arguably the most intractable aspect of Israel’s future for any new government is its stance toward Iran. Oct. 7 and the subsequent genocide further entrenched the prevailing doctrine: maintaining "forward defense” and using overwhelming force as deterrence against regional adversaries.
Prime Minister Netanyahu has repeatedly made clear his ambitions extend beyond containment: "There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all: overthrow the regime in Iran,” he declared at a recent graduation for military officers, describing Iran as the "head of the venomous octopus” that threatens Israeli and regional security.
Eisenkot, though less fiery in his rhetoric, has promised no dramatic departure from this approach.
As the U.S. continues its policy of pressuring Tehran, a State Department spokesperson reiterated, "as long as Iran devotes its energy revenues to financing attacks on our allies, supporting terrorism around the world, and pursuing other destabilizing actions, we will use all the tools at our disposal to hold the regime accountable.”
The Trump administration also reiterated its opposition to the annexation of the West Bank, describing a "stable West Bank” as crucial to Israeli security and regional peace.
Despite the alarm Netanyahu provokes among Arab leaders – many of whom fear his expansionist agenda – there is a begrudging acknowledgment that his hard line against Iran aligns with their own security calculations.
"Netanyahu’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank, Syria and Lebanon are damaging,” said Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Center. "As for Iran, a settlement is needed before the conflict escalates further. If Iran’s role is not curbed, the region could be heading toward 50 years of Iranian hegemony.”
Michael Young of the Carnegie Middle East Center notes that underlying Israeli consensus "reduces the scope for big policy shifts.” Recent years have seen the emergence of a rough stalemate: Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza weakened, but not eliminated, and Iran’s broader regional influence endures. The Iranians, he argues, bet they can outlast their opponents and retain their ambitions, including pursuit of a nuclear deterrent.
"This is a quagmire,” Young said. "The Iranians can outlast Trump.”
The contours of likely government coalitions reinforce the direction of policy. Netanyahu’s current government depends on support from far-right parties led by settler activists Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who openly promote annexation and have been sanctioned in some Western capitals for encouraging settler violence. The coalition also includes ultra-Orthodox parties, who demand broad exemptions from military service.
Eisenkot, by contrast, would need to rely on right-wing parties less radical than Netanyahu’s allies, and possibly the Democrats’ small center-left faction. Neither candidate, however, is expected to seek support from Arab-led parties, and Eisenkot’s opposition to military exemptions further complicates coalition arithmetic.
For the region – whether in Tehran, Riyadh, or Ramallah – Tuesday’s ballot is viewed not as a potential turning point, but as a test of whether a long confrontation is becoming permanent. "From Tehran to Riyadh, Tuesday's election is not seen as a potential turning point but as a test of whether the Middle East is settling into a long confrontation, where wars ebb and flow while the underlying conflicts are unresolved,” said one observer.
The coming days may deliver a new Israeli prime minister – or reaffirm Netanyahu’s long rule – but the strategic posture toward Palestinians, Iran, and the wider Middle East, will likely remain unchanged. For many, the only open question is whether the next government chooses to escalate existing conflicts or simply maintain the status quo.

articles.title: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes  The GuardianIsrael expands expulsions in occupied West Bank to cement control  Al JazeeraIsraeli military closing West Bank crossings ahead of upcoming elections as massive operation continues  CBS NewsWest Bank: Hebron crackdown displaces thousands, Türk warns of ethnic cleansing  UN NewsBulldozers tear down home as Israel cracks down in the West...
articles.full_text:
Hebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.
A gun attack on an Israeli military checkpoint on Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition is narrowly trailing with two days of campaigning left.
They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale the West Bank has not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.
Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.
As the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.
The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.
Ahmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.
“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”
At midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.
He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.
The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.
Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.
“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.
Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.
“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”
By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.
In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.
The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.
“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.
By Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.
“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.
“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”

Hundreds of protesters stormed the Roman Colosseum and clashed with police at the historic gates as the demonstrations in France spread to Italy over the weekend.
The protesters, many of them young and waving Palestinian flags, were seen cheering and yelling inside the 2,000-year-old arena during the demonstrations in Rome as security forces pushed them out.
The tense scene was one of many across the country on Saturday as thousands marched in the streets of Rome, Milan, Turin and other cities to protest the current cost-of-living crisis and the ongoing war in Gaza.
The Colosseum had notably upped its security ahead of the protest following months of clashes with tourists running wild in the historic site, with the arena declared a security “red zone” last month.
Along with the clashes at the Colosseum, officials reported another violent confrontation with protesters near the Piazza della Repubblica, with police deploying tear gas and water cannons.
In Milan, protesters dumped manure outside the country’s energy regulator and burned an oversized electricity bill.
Many stores in the city boarded up their windows to avoid last week’s looting where protesters were caught making off with luxury goods in France.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni sent about 500 soldiers to Milan to assist the 5,000 officers deployed to the area.
The soldiers, however, were not equipped with pepper spray or Tasers, only plastic restraint ties to help arrest rowdy protesters, Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said.
The protests in Italy mimic the demonstrations that broke out in France last month and have spread across Europe over the continent’s economic woes.
Along with Italy, large demonstrations were also reported in the capitals of Spain, Portugal and Albania.

Summary US President Donald Trump says Washington faces a choice between reaching an agreement with Iran and taking decisive action, while claiming major damage to its nuclear facilities.
WASHINGTON (Dunya News) — US President Donald Trump has said Washington must choose between reaching an agreement with Iran and taking decisive action against the country, as tensions between the two sides continue.
In an interview with Fox News, Trump framed the issue as a choice between striking a deal with Tehran and pursuing an approach aimed at ending the Iranian threat permanently.
The US president claimed that Iran had made little significant progress regarding its nuclear facilities and that most of the country’s nuclear infrastructure had been destroyed.
Trump also said the United States was closely monitoring activities at locations he identified as Pickaxe Mountain and Mount Al-Fas in Iran.
He criticised the nuclear agreement negotiated under former US President Barack Obama, describing it as the worst deal.
The 2015 nuclear agreement, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), placed restrictions on Iran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief. The United States withdrew from the agreement in 2018 during Trump’s first presidency.
Trump claims control over Strait of Hormuz
Discussing maritime security, Trump claimed that the United States had complete control over the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically important waterway through which a substantial share of global oil supplies normally passes.
He also asserted that commercial activity through the strait had increased compared with the period before the war.
The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and serves as a critical route for oil and gas shipments from major Gulf energy producers.
Any sustained disruption to shipping through the passage could affect global energy markets, transportation costs and oil prices.
Oil prices expected to fall after war, Trump says
Trump predicted that oil prices would fall sharply once the war ended.
His remarks come amid continued uncertainty over the conflict, Iran’s nuclear programme and the security of energy infrastructure and maritime routes in the region.
A potential agreement between Washington and Tehran could have implications for regional security, sanctions and international energy markets. However, the president’s statements did not establish whether a new agreement was imminent or what specific terms any proposed deal might contain.

articles.title: Time for Saudi Clarity on Normalization with Israel - Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

articles.full_text:
The Mecca Pact and the Limits of American Guarantees
Why Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey are joining forces on regional security.
- Alper Coşkun, Amr Hamzawy
The U.S. midterm elections signal the opening of a narrow window for bold Saudi diplomacy on Palestine.
Saudi policy on Palestine/Israel is officially set by the Arab Peace Initiative (API) of 2002, which offered normalization between Israel and the Arab world in exchange for Palestinian statehood and a just settlement for Palestinian refugees. Under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS), however, the kingdom has maintained greater ambiguity about its ultimate aims, publicly asserting support for the API while privately entertaining the idea of Saudi Arabia–Israel normalization. For a time, this ambiguity served Saudi Arabia by encouraging successive U.S. administrations to court the kingdom with various sweeteners. As the kingdom has recognized, any deal would still require a face-saving Palestinian component, which could be spun as preserving Palestinian national aspirations. However, Saudi Arabia would not insist on full statehood as a precondition.
This ambiguity is no longer in Saudi interests—or those of regional peace and stability, if it ever has been. The strategic landscape of the Middle East has shifted in the wake of the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023; Israel’s military response, including what the Saudi government and MBS subsequently labeled a genocide; and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Scenes of devastation in Gaza and Lebanon have inflamed Arab (and Saudi) public opinion, while years of Israeli belligerence toward the country’s neighbors and dismissiveness toward Saudi Arabia have called into question the direct value of normalization. Nor is it clear that normalization would add much to Saudi-U.S. ties. The kingdom has already secured significant economic and security advantages from the United States even in the absence of normalization, including support for a civil nuclear program.
Ambiguity is no longer in Saudi interests—or those of regional peace and stability, if it ever has been.
Despite this reality, supporters of normalization still argue that the United States should either encourage or coerce Saudi Arabia to establish ties with Israel. U.S. President Donald Trump, for example, intervened last-minute to condition a bilateral nuclear technology deal on the kingdom joining the Abraham Accords, the framework that established open ties between Israel and Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2020. Proponents of normalization invariably dismiss the significance of Palestinian statehood, either by arguing that Saudi Arabia will settle for less or by ignoring Palestinians entirely. A whisper campaign from anonymous U.S. and Israeli sources has also suggested Saudi Arabia may need Israeli security assistance to confront Houthi forces in Yemen.
These arguments misread new Saudi red lines regarding the kingdom’s support for Palestinian national aspirations and its concerns about Israeli and Iranian regional belligerence. Even MBS may now value Palestinian statehood in its own right, rather than as a bargaining chip with the United States or as a public relations talking point within the Arab world. Changing regional realities, as well as public opinion shifts in the United States and abroad, make a clear statement of Saudi aims and interests more advantageous. By working to shape the diplomatic agenda on Palestinian statehood, Saudi Arabia can both reinforce its credibility and demonstrate its commitment to Palestinian self-determination.1
Definitive Saudi action now could help redraw the geopolitical map and remove a major driver of Middle East conflicts, whereas simply playing defense against Iranian, Israeli, U.S., and Houthi aims cannot. Flipping the script on normalization, by putting the Trump administration on notice of Saudi Arabia’s requirement that Israel first end its occupation over the Palestinian territories, is certain to cause short-term Saudi-U.S. tension. The alternative, however, means accepting Israel’s campaign to ethnically cleanse Gaza and much of the West Bank, strengthening the legitimacy of political actors in Sanaa and Tehran, and undermining Saudi Arabia’s credibility.
The kingdom has a limited window to seize the initiative between election dynamics in the United States and Israel, the mounting costs of war in the Gulf, and Israeli efforts to establish new facts on the ground in Palestine. Close coordination with Palestinian leadership is essential to both the political success of the project and its perceived legitimacy in the eyes of other regional actors and Arab constituencies. The kingdom could achieve diplomatic traction by partnering with other stakeholders in Europe and the region through existing mechanisms such as the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two-State Solution. A broad coalition, buoyed by international frustration over the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, could provide political cover and seasoned diplomacy in addressing one of the region’s thorniest and longest-standing challenges. While overtly pressing for Palestinian statehood is not risk-free, Saudi Arabia is well positioned to argue that a true “grand bargain” would both neutralize an important Iranian talking point and offer a better chance for Trump to claim a diplomatic win by the end of his term—so long as he is willing to deploy pressure on Israel.
Definitive Saudi action now could help redraw the geopolitical map and remove a major driver of Middle East conflicts.
Understand the world with the latest from our scholars around the world.
From the outset of U.S.-Saudi relations through the mid-2010s, the kingdom’s policy toward the Palestinian issue was a balancing act: signaling enough support for the cause to court domestic and regional audiences, while also indicating enough pragmatism to keep the issue from hindering growing security ties with the United States.2 Still, through the early 1970s, the kingdom generally played a less prominent role than the so-called frontline states of Egypt, Syria, and Jordan. After 1948, Saudi rulers generally treated Israel’s existence as an established fact in private, while making contributions to the United Nations Relief and Works Agency in support of Palestinian refugees and (after its formation in 1964) the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).3
Developments in the 1970s pushed Saudi Arabia to play a more prominent regional role, while generating expectations among Palestinian leaders that the kingdom could wield significant leverage on their behalf. Having tested the efficacy of an oil embargo amid the 1967 Arab-Israeli War, various Arab states again deployed that leverage in response to U.S. support for Israel during the 1973 Arab-Israeli War. While Saudi Arabia’s King Faisal initially resisted joining in, he eventually became the public face of “the oil weapon.”4 The Arab oil embargo proved to Arab constituencies across the Middle East—in particular, Palestinians within the occupied territories and in host Arab countries—that Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states had meaningful agency on the world stage, if they chose to deploy it.
For the time being, however, Saudi Arabia adopted the role of regional coordinator, working to maintain the Arab consensus on the Palestinian issue while signaling its “pragmatism” toward the United States. After the Camp David Accords established diplomatic relations between Egypt and Israel, this meant bowing to other Arab states in boycotting Egypt and relocating the Arab League headquarters to Tunisia as punishment. Saudi Crown Prince Fahad also offered his own proposal for addressing Palestinian national aspirations, which held out the possibility of “peace between all states of the region” conditioned on what would become the API formulation: an end to the occupation, support for the right of return, and the establishment of an independent Palestinian state.
Decades later, the Saudi-backed API would offer “normal relations” between Israel and all Arab states in exchange for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state. Jordan had tried advancing a similar plan years earlier. However, it was the second Palestinian uprising against the Israeli occupation (following Israeli prime minister Ariel Sharon’s provocative tour of the Al Aqsa mosque compound in 2000) and the ensuing violence that would give the offer of Arab normalization with Israel in exchange for an end to the occupation some urgency.5 Support for the API also provided Saudi Arabia a way to begin to repair the damage done to the kingdom on the international stage by the role some Saudi citizens played in the 9/11 terrorist attacks on U.S. soil.
Saudi officials were also motivated by concern at the reaction of Arab (and Saudi) public opinion to images of embattled Muslims in Jerusalem—broadcast region-wide by Qatar’s newly established Al Jazeera television station. Even before the 9/11 attacks, Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah privately accused the George W. Bush administration of setting the U.S. national interest “100-percent based on Sharon” and doing little to restrain Israeli violence, especially in Jerusalem. Championing the API was thus a way for the Saudi monarchy to demonstrate regional leadership and burnish its legitimacy at home.
Saudi support for ending Israeli occupation, however, remained limited to broad proposals and occasional efforts to mediate intra-Palestinian disputes. Crown Prince Abdullah helped secure collective Arab support for the API and subsequently lobbied Bush on its importance, ensuring that the U.S. administration’s subsequent road map for a comprehensive resolution to the Arab-Israeli conflict referenced “the initiative of Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah” as part of the basis for a just settlement. At the same time, Abdullah’s advisors made it clear that Saudi lobbying would not be backed up with overt pressure like the “oil weapon.”

Rep. Nancy Mace pushed back against Barack Obama's claim that Iran did not have a nuclear weapon because of his deal.
On Saturday, former US President Obama held a campaign rally in Detroit ahead of the midterms. During his speech, he took aim at Trump and his administration for high gas prices. According to a video of his address shared on his YouTube channel, Obama argued that the current administration's actions were "directly responsible for rising costs." He said that Trump made a "series of bad decisions" and blamed him for starting an "unnecessary war."
"Of course, Iran didn't have nuclear weapons. We had curbed their nuclear program because I put in place a deal that everybody acknowledged had kept them from getting nukes. I didn't have to fire a missile. I engaged in diplomacy," he said.
For those unaware, Obama was talking about the JCPOA, which his administration signed with Iran in 2015. However, Trump later withdrew from the deal in 2018, per CNN. At the time, Trump called the agreement "defective at its core."
On Monday, GOP lawmaker Nancy Mace, who herself voiced opposition to the continued military conflict with Iran, shared her reaction to Barack Obama's claim in an X post. Mace posted:
"I don't agree with the Iran war, but I also don't believe in revisionist history. Obama's comments are complete nonsense. Iran never possessed a nuclear weapon - before his deal or after. The JCPOA was a temporary pause with sunset clauses that left Tehran’s enrichment infrastructure intact, legitimized their nuclear program, and handed them a path to a nuclear bomb after 10 to 15 years. It also unlocked tens of billions in sanctions relief that funded the regime’s terror proxies. 'Everybody acknowledges' it worked? Basic facts do not. Temporary diplomacy that enriches a terrorist regime isn’t strength - it’s weakness and it's a lie."
During his campaign rally in Michigan on Sunday, President Trump justified his decision to withdraw from the JCPOA and defended his actions against Iran. He alleged that the JCPOA was a "road to Iran having a nuclear weapon." He added:
"It was the worst agreement and the most dangerous agreement I've ever seen. And we obliterated Iran's nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury."
Trump claimed that the US has "defeated" Iran militarily and financially and said that Washington is now ensuring that Tehran "will never have" a nuclear weapon. He went on to claim that the war would end "quite soon."
Barack Obama says Iran is in a better position than before the war started
In his Saturday speech, after crediting the JCPOA with keeping nukes away from Iran, the former POTUS questioned how the ongoing war has benefited the US. He said:
"Look 7 months later, how's that war going? Our allies and bases have been attacked. American soldiers have been killed. Hundreds of Americans have been wounded. We've run down our stock of missiles dangerously low. And this is the thing. Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to get to the world. So, they're in a stronger strategic position now than before the war started."
Obama stated that the ongoing war with Iran is the "reason" for high oil and diesel prices and stressed that it is not over yet.
Later in his speech, the former president also lashed out at Trump over his tariff war with Canada.

articles.title: Intel to acquire Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3 billion - CTech
articles.summary: Intel to acquire Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3 billion  CTech
articles.full_text:
The deal marks a record acquisition in the quantum computing industry and a major exit for Israel’s tech sector, with Classiq’s founders, employees and early investors poised for substantial returns.
The first major exit for Israel’s quantum industry: Classiq, a developer of operating systems for quantum computers, is being acquired by Intel for $2.3 billion in a combination of cash and stock. The deal would make Classiq the most expensive quantum company acquisition to date, by a significant margin. The previous record was set last year, when IonQ acquired Oxford Ionics for $1 billion.
The transaction also marks a major acquisition for Intel, which paid approximately $1 billion for Israeli mobility company Moovit six years ago and $2 billion for Habana Labs a year earlier. Intel has made other acquisitions since then, including the Israeli company Granulate, but those deals were valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Intel has not acquired another Israeli company since the Granulate deal in 2022.
For Israelis accustomed to multibillion-dollar exits in cybersecurity, $2.3 billion might not seem particularly large. In quantum computing, however, it represents a landmark deal. Despite the excitement surrounding the field, quantum computers have yet to achieve widespread practical commercial use. There are currently only 117 quantum computers worldwide, and they remain prohibitively expensive and largely inaccessible.
Quantum computing has shown promise for decades, and the field has recorded several significant breakthroughs over the past two years. Yet it has not experienced its own “ChatGPT moment,” a breakthrough that would bring the technology into widespread use.
Despite its small size, Israel is considered one of the world’s five leading countries in quantum computing, both in the number of companies operating in the field and in the volume of private investment. Intel’s acquisition of Classiq for more than $2 billion could draw greater investor attention to Israel and provide another catalyst for the development of its quantum industry.
The deal recalls Intel’s acquisition of Mobileye, the autonomous-driving company founded by Amnon Shashua, a decade ago. That transaction helped trigger a wave of investment in Israeli companies in the sector. The hope is that Classiq’s exit will have a similar effect, with even better long-term results for the industry.
For Classiq’s founders, employees and investors, the acquisition represents an impressive exit for a company founded just six years ago. Classiq currently employs around 150 people. Employees collectively hold 10% of the company’s shares, equivalent to $230 million at the acquisition price, although the proceeds will vary among individuals. Intel has also allocated more than $100 million in retention grants to encourage employees to remain with the company.
Classiq was founded by Nir Minerbi, Amir Naveh and his father, Prof. Yehuda Naveh. Minerbi is the CEO, Amir Naveh is the CPO, and Yehuda Naveh is the CTO. Minerbi and the younger Naveh are graduates of the Israel Defense Forces’ Talpiot program, as are many of the company’s employees. Yehuda Naveh previously held a senior position at IBM’s Israeli development center. Each of the three founders is expected to receive between $80 million and $100 million from the deal.
Classiq generates revenue, but its annual revenue remains in the tens of millions of dollars, well below an annual run rate of $100 million. The acquisition price therefore represents a substantial valuation multiple for a relatively young company.
Classiq occupies a distinctive position in the quantum computing industry. It develops software that serves as an operating system for quantum computers, bridging the gap between complex hardware and the people and organizations seeking to use it. The company’s ambition is to become the “Windows” of quantum computing.
IBM, a pioneer in quantum computing, is its main competitor. Estimates suggest that Classiq has already surpassed IBM in market share, although the companies’ positions depend on how that market is measured. Classiq’s software is hardware-agnostic, meaning it is designed to work across different quantum computing platforms rather than being tied to a single manufacturer.
Its customers span several industries, including banking, automotive and pharmaceuticals. They include BMW, Rolls-Royce, HSBC, Deloitte, Toshiba and Citi.
Classiq has raised approximately $200 million to date, making the acquisition a profitable outcome for its investors as well. Its most recent funding round, a $110 million raise in 2025, valued the company at an estimated $600 million to $700 million, far below the acquisition price.
Entrée Capital, which led Classiq’s pre-seed round and is its largest shareholder, stands to gain the most. The fund is expected to receive more than $300 million on an investment of just a few million dollars. Team8 Capital, the company’s second-largest shareholder, holds a 9% stake.
The deal is also expected to benefit Israeli savers through The Phoenix, which holds a 7.5% stake in Classiq. Unlike many recent Israeli technology exits, most of which have involved cybersecurity companies, Classiq is incorporated in Israel. The state is therefore expected to collect tax revenue from the transaction beyond the taxes paid by founders and employees who sell their shares.
However, because a significant portion of the consideration is in Intel stock, not all the proceeds will be realized immediately in cash.
One of Classiq’s private investors is Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s current CEO, who has led the chipmaker’s turnaround over the past year and a half. Tan invested in Classiq personally before becoming CEO of the company now acquiring the startup. According to sources close to Classiq, he recused himself from discussions concerning the acquisition.
Other notable investors include NightDragon, a fund led by Dave DeWalt, who previously headed cybersecurity company McAfee.
Until recently, Classiq had been exploring a potential IPO on Wall Street, where several quantum computing companies have gone public over the past year. Most entered the public markets through mergers with special-purpose acquisition companies, or SPACs, and their subsequent share-price performance has been weak in recent months.
The only company to go public through a traditional IPO was Quantinuum, which debuted at a peak valuation of $15 billion. It has since lost 35% of its value and is currently valued at approximately $9.5 billion. IonQ, which went public through a SPAC merger in 2021, is now the most highly valued publicly traded quantum company, with a market capitalization of around $13 billion.
At $2.3 billion, the Classiq acquisition would place the Israeli company among the five most highly valued businesses in the global quantum computing sector. The valuation also illustrates the premium Intel is willing to pay for a company operating in a field that has yet to reach broad commercial adoption.
Like many founders, Minerbi and Naveh had spoken of global expansion and building an independent company. But with Intel offering $2.3 billion for a business that had raised approximately $200 million and was valued at $600 million to $700 million in its latest funding round, the acquisition represents a substantial outcome for its shareholders and a major milestone for Israel’s quantum industry.

articles.title: Salesforce acquires Israeli analytics startup Loops - The Ticker
