Salesforce Inc., a leading customer management company, signed an agreement to acquire the Israeli artificial intelligence startup Loops on Oct. 12. Salesforce provides software that helps businesses improve their processes by tracking sales, managing customer data and handling customer-service requests.
According to a case study on Salesforce’s customer, Publisher Wiley, Wiley, “sees 213% return on investment” as it implements Agentforce to answer questions about accessing accounts, resetting passwords and payment issues by directing users to relevant resources. Nevertheless, the acquisition of Loops will allow Salesforce to expand its machine learning capabilities and integrate them with its existing software.
For businesses, Loops aids companies with management decisions by helping them understand the factors driving results. Its technology identifies and analyzes changes in performance and provides feedback on which updates may be helping or hurting results.
Salesforce envisions that new AI-powered tools will help customers move toward becoming full agentic analytics enterprises. For Salesforce, its integration of Loops into Tableau will go beyond its current strategy, moving from insight to action in the flow of work.
The new data visualization and analytics features will monitor businesses’ performance indicators, explain why metrics change and identify improvement opportunities by leveraging machine learning models. Salesforce clients will be able to identify trends and explore unusual changes more quickly.
In a case study published by Loops, the AI-powered platform Atera improved conversion rates after receiving Loops’ insights on the primary cause of a performance decline. Its Release Impact analysis model measured changes in business metrics, enabling Atera’s team to learn rapidly from previous iterations and react accordingly to achieve success.
With a Salesforce integration, the insights that Loops can provide through tools like Slack can reduce manual analysis and help teams respond to problems and opportunities more promptly.
Although Salesforce states that it incorporates human rights into business decisions, the announcement of the Loops acquisition did mention the ongoing conflicts involving Israel.
Amid intense ethical questioning of U.S. business relationships with Israel, Loops will become the 10th Israeli company acquired by Salesforce. The company’s recent Israeli acquisitions include
OwnBackup for cloud-based data backup solutions, Doti AI for agentic enterprise search and Spindle AI for agentic analytics in 2025.
The U.S. free-trade agreement with Israel, which has been in effect since 1985, serves as the basis for increasing mutual trade and investment between the two countries. As Israel specializes in the creation of sophisticated technologies, such as AI tools, cybersecurity and other enterprise software, the U.S. benefits from investments and acquisitions by building substantial capital, partnerships and customer bases. Salesforce’s continued acquisitions of Israeli technologies, including Loops, illustrate the persistence of these investment ties amid the current conflict.
While the deal was estimated to be worth $30 million, Salesforce has not disclosed the final purchase price, but the company’s leadership is optimistic about the acquisition’s potential to reach more customers. According to Yahoo Finance, the deal is expected to close this November, during the company’s 2027 fiscal year.

articles.title: Israel committing crimes against humanity in occupied West Bank: UN - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Israel committing crimes against humanity in occupied West Bank: UN  Al JazeeraIsrael Has Committed Genocidal Acts in Gaza Since Cease-Fire, U.N. Human Rights Panel Says  The New York TimesUN inquiry says Israel kept committing genocide in Gaza after truce  Reuters'Legitimazes Jihad': Foreign Affairs Ministry slams UN report accusing Israel of genocide  The Jerusalem PostUN-commissioned experts say Gaza ceasefire has not stopped Israel from committing geno...
articles.full_text:
A United Nations commission of inquiry has accused Israel of committing crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape, while also continuing “to commit genocide in Gaza” despite a ceasefire brokered by the United States.
The report, published on Monday by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, examined killings and physical and mental harm inflicted by state actors from October 7, 2023, through September of this year.
It was released the day before Israel’s general election.
The commission found that the situation in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, had “deteriorated gravely” since the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
It said Israeli military operations, reinforced by sustained violence by settlers, amounted to a “widespread and systematic attack” on civilians, and that Israeli authorities “intended to collectively punish” residents of the occupied West Bank for the Hamas-led attack on Israel.
“The Israeli authorities and forces have committed the crimes against humanity of extermination, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence in the West Bank, as well as persecution based on intersecting discriminatory grounds, with nationality, race and ethnicity at its core,” the report said.
Extermination
The commission also found a sharp rise in deaths from air strikes in the territory.
Six Palestinians were killed in air attacks in the occupied West Bank from 2008 to October 6, 2023, it said, compared with 254 from October 7, 2023, to September 30, 2026.
“The intentional killing and injuring of Palestinian civilians and destruction of homes in the West Bank combined with Israel’s persistent denial of responsibility form part of a broader strategy to exterminate and displace Palestinians and impose conditions of life that are unlivable,” said Srinivasan Muralidhar, the commission’s chair.
“Meanwhile, Israel’s expansion of territorial control in Gaza continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinian civilians who approach or cross” the so-called Yellow Line that demarcates Israeli-controlled areas in the enclave, he said.
Israel’s mission in Geneva called the report part of the commission’s “misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel and portray its very existence as criminal”.
“The international community must reject these distortions, repudiate the commission’s findings and demand its immediate dissolution,” the mission said in a statement.
Continued genocide
The commission, which does not speak for the UN as a whole, first concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza during the war that followed the October 7 attacks. Israel has flatly rejected the UN commission’s finding.
In its new report, the commission said Israeli forces had continued to commit “genocidal acts” against Palestinians in Gaza despite the ceasefire brokered by the US last October, with attacks intended to “destroy the Palestinian people, in whole or in part”.
At least five Palestinians, including a seven-year-old girl, were killed in Israeli air attacks across Gaza on Monday, according to medical officials there. The Gaza Health Ministry says at least 74,500 people have been killed in the genocidal war, which has displaced nearly all of the territory’s population.
The report also examined abuses by Palestinian security forces. It found that the Palestinian Authority had targeted people who voiced dissent, and that the killing and wounding of journalists and human rights defenders had steadily narrowed space for civil society.
The three-member commission was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021.
Navi Pillay, a former South African High Court judge who led it until last November, won the Nobel Peace Prize this month.
West Bank lockdown
The report was released as Israeli forces carried out a crackdown in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron after a shooting near the city last week. Israel imposed a lockdown on Hebron on Friday, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans to extend it across the entire West Bank.
Later on Monday, Volker Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights, condemned the Hebron operation. He said threats to empty and erase neighbourhoods raised “serious concerns of ethnic cleansing”.
According to Turk, the lockdown had already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians, led to the demolition of homes and prevented residents from moving freely.
“The sweeping steps taken raise grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate use of force – which must end,” he said.
“The Israeli lockdown is confining many to their homes and their immediate neighbourhoods. Declarations by senior Israeli government officials indicate that the measures implemented are punitive in nature and designed to instil fear. This is unacceptable,” Turk added.
Some Israeli ministers have previously called for the occupied West Bank and Gaza to be ethnically cleansed.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told Ynet News last month that Israel should “go to war” in the occupied territory and repeat what it “did in Gaza”. He added that Israeli forces had “cleared out” Palestinian refugee camps in the occupied West Bank.
Turk insisted that people displaced under the clampdown must be allowed to return home and that “Israel must ensure compensation and reparation for unlawful evictions and demolitions”.
“Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law,” he said.

articles.title: Delegations meet in Iran with the Middle East on edge over potential for renewed fighting - PBS
articles.summary: Delegations meet in Iran with the Middle East on edge over potential for renewed fighting  PBS
articles.full_text:
CAIRO (AP) — High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war, Iran's Foreign Ministry said.
The talks came as many in Iran are anxious about a possible return to all-out war. Israeli and American leaders have been sharpening their threats before elections in both countries, while Iranian leaders have remained defiant.
Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey's intelligence service, met with Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington.
The war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also topics of the talks, according to two regional officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak with reporters.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran that the agenda for the meeting wasn't set, but the talks would "undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security." Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said during the talks Monday that Iran supports any agreement that would deepen regional cooperation, resolve differences and make greater use of the shared resources and capabilities of Islamic countries.
Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find "ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability."
Qatari mediators also traveled to Tehran on Sunday, working in coordination with the United States, as part of efforts to de-escalate regional tensions, according to a regional official speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.
Pakistan and Qatar helped broker an agreement in June aimed at having Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, ending a U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and opening negotiations on a broader settlement addressing Iran's nuclear program. The deal unraveled quickly, however, as both sides renewed attacks.
Iran and Israel trade accusations
With worries about renewed fighting before Israel's election on Tuesday and the U.S. midterm election on Nov. 3, Baghaei said over the weekend that Iran hadn't closed the window of diplomacy and that messages were being passed to the United States through intermediaries.
With negotiations long stalled, he said that the U.S. appears to be persisting in unilateral demands and that U.S. President Donald Trump and other American officials repeatedly use the phrase "complete surrender," which Baghaei said that no Iranian accepts.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, repeated his warning on Sunday that Iran or its proxies could launch an attack before the close election to disrupt the vote, citing intelligence.
"The (military) is ready both to defend and to strike," he said in a video statement. "You will suffer disproportionate blows far greater than you can imagine."
Israel's Channel 12 reported Sunday night that Netanyahu and his military chief of staff clashed over an instruction by Netanyahu to carry out an "action" that the army believes could quickly trigger a resumption of the conflict with Iran.
Netanyahu's office later described the report as "fake news." In a post on X, Defense Minister Israel Katz said that reports about "rifts between the political leadership and the IDF concerning Iran are completely baseless and false."
"I state unequivocally that there has been no intention by Israel of initiating an attack on Iran before the elections in Israel," Katz said. "We made it clear that should Iran attack Israel, we would respond with great force."
In Tehran, when asked whether Iran was planning attacks, Baghaei on Monday only said that "the Israeli regime is highly skilled at carrying out false-flag operations."
"The Islamic Republic of Iran will not hesitate to exercise its inherent right to self-defense to protect Iran's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence," he said.
Front in the Iran war widens
Yemen has become a widening front in the Iran war that began in February, with the Houthis increasingly launching attacks on Saudi Arabia because it supports Yemen's internationally recognized government battling the rebels.
The conflict has intensified since forces from the internationally recognized government and Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that largely stopped the fighting in the country's civil war.
Early Monday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said that the rebel group had fired ballistic missiles at military gatherings and weapons depots belonging to Saudi-backed government forces in Aden and Lahj provinces. He said that the attacks destroyed military equipment and caused casualties, but didn't provide evidence. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the information.
Residents in Houthi-held Sanaa and on the Red Sea coast reported a series of explosions.
Houthi media said that airstrikes targeted a solar power system and a water well in Sanaa, but offered no proof. In the port city of Mokha, recently seized by the Houthis, residents said that rockets hit several buildings, including a hospital.
Houthi-run al-Masirah channel also reported strikes in Saada, in northern Yemen, and in southwestern Taiz province, where the rebels and Saudi-backed government forces have been fighting for weeks.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said that an operation in Houthi-controlled territory destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and other missile storage.
Meanwhile, Egypt's parliament on Monday approved a request from President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi to provide military support to Saudi Arabia to help defend against Houthi attacks.
Victoria Eastwood and Fatma Khaled in Cairo, Natalie Melzer in Tel Aviv, Israel, Munir Ahmed in Islamabad, Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen, and David Rising in Bangkok, contributed to this report.

articles.title: What are the sources of LNG supply for Vietnam's electricity production? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: What are the sources of LNG supply for Vietnam's electricity production?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, Vietnam has several options for importing liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Middle East, Asia-Pacific, and Russia. However, each source of supply has its own advantages and risks.
The revised Power Development Plan VIII anticipates the development of 15 LNG power projects with a total capacity of over 25.6 GW. Therefore, ensuring a stable and long-term supply of LNG at competitive prices is a critical requirement for the efficient operation of these projects, contributing to national energy security.
Global LNG supply continues to expand.
According to a report by the Ministry of Industry and Trade assessing the potential for LNG imports for electricity production, global natural gas reserves are expected to reach approximately 209 trillion cubic meters by the end of 2024. Of this, Russia has the largest reserves with nearly 47 trillion cubic meters, followed by Iran with nearly 34 trillion cubic meters, Qatar with 23.8 trillion cubic meters, and the United States with nearly 18 trillion cubic meters.
The United States has been the world's largest producer of natural gas for many years, with production reaching 925-1,073 billion cubic meters per year between 2020 and 2025. Russia ranks second, maintaining production of 586-702 billion cubic meters per year. Other major gas producers include Canada, Norway , Iran, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and China.
Alongside exploration activities, global LNG production capacity continues to expand. By the end of 2025, total liquefaction capacity is expected to reach 524.5 million tonnes per year, an increase of 30.1 million tonnes compared to 2024. The United States, Australia, and Qatar are among the world's leading liquefaction capacity providers.
In 2025 alone, the United States exported 110.74 million tons of LNG, accounting for approximately 25% of total global LNG production. This was followed by Qatar with 81.5 million tons, Australia with 80.3 million tons, Russia with 30.5 million tons, and Malaysia with 28.8 million tons.
Conversely, around 50 countries are expected to import LNG in 2025, primarily concentrated in Asia and Europe. China continues to be the largest import market with 69.77 million tons, although this is down 8.9 million tons from the previous year. Other major markets include Japan , Taiwan, and France.
Currently, Vietnam has the Thi Vai LNG terminal with a receiving capacity of 1 million tons/year, expected to be increased to 3 million tons/year, and the Cai Mep LNG port with a capacity of approximately 3 million tons/year.
Besides infrastructure investment, long-term LNG supply contracts have also been signed, including a contract with Shell to supply approximately 400,000 tons of LNG per year from 2027 to 2031.
The Middle East has significant potential to supply LNG.
According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Middle East, especially Qatar, has the potential to become a major source of LNG for Vietnam thanks to its abundant reserves, large production capacity, and well-developed export infrastructure.
In 2025, LNG from Qatar will account for approximately 26.4% of Vietnam's total LNG imports.
Qatar's LNG production is concentrated in the industrial city of Ras Laffan, which has a large-scale LNG liquefaction and export infrastructure, combined with CO2 capture and storage facilities.
You may also like
Qatar is developing the North Field East and North Field South projects, which are expected to increase total liquefaction capacity to approximately 142 million tonnes per year by 2030.
In terms of transportation, the distance from Qatar to Vietnam is greater than from Indonesia, Malaysia, and Russia, but shorter than shipping routes from the United States.
However, LNG supplies from the Middle East also pose geopolitical risks. LNG exports from Qatar to Vietnam must pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a shipping lane sensitive to political and security instability in the region.
This necessitates a balance between economies of scale and the ability to ensure stable transportation when choosing to import LNG from the Middle East.
Australia and Malaysia have advantages in transportation.
Besides the Middle East, the Asia-Pacific region has many potential LNG suppliers for Vietnam, notably Australia, Malaysia, and Indonesia.
Australia has natural gas reserves of approximately 4 trillion cubic meters. Although significantly lower than Qatar, the country remains one of the world's largest exporters of LNG.
In 2025, Australia will export 80.3 million tonnes of LNG, ranking third globally, accounting for nearly 19% of global exports and roughly matching Qatar's production.
Major LNG projects are concentrated in Western Australia, including North West Shelf LNG with a capacity of 16.9 million tonnes/year, Gorgon LNG with 15.6 million tonnes/year, and Wheatstone LNG with 8.9 million tonnes/year.
Australia's advantage lies in its export port system located on international shipping routes, facilitating the transportation of LNG to Asian markets, including Vietnam. Importantly, these shipping routes do not pass through geopolitical bottlenecks such as the Strait of Hormuz.
However, Australia's future LNG export capacity may be impacted by domestic energy security policies, including the Australian Gas Security Mechanism (ADGSM).
For Malaysia, the biggest advantage is its geographical proximity to Vietnam.
In 2025, Malaysia exported 28.8 million tons of LNG, ranking fifth in the world. The country's LNG infrastructure is mainly concentrated in the Bintulu complex in Sarawak state.
The shipping distance from Bintulu to the Southeast region of Vietnam is only about 1,000-1,500 nautical miles, making it one of the shortest shipping routes among international LNG suppliers.
However, the long-term outlook for LNG imports from Malaysia also faces challenges. According to information cited by the Ministry of Industry and Trade from the International Energy Agency (IEA), some of Malaysia's traditional gas fields have entered a decline phase, while domestic gas demand tends to increase.
You may also like
Therefore, Malaysia's LNG exports are projected to increase slowly or decrease slightly in the long term unless more large-scale gas projects come online.
Supply from Russia is affected by sanctions.
Russia possesses the world's largest natural gas reserves, with nearly 47 trillion cubic meters, accounting for approximately 21% of total global reserves.
Russia's gas resources are mainly located in Siberia, the Yamal Peninsula, and Sakhalin Island. Average annual production is approximately 640-650 billion cubic meters.
Previously, Russian natural gas was primarily exported to Europe via pipelines. However, after 2022, as European demand for Russian gas declined sharply, Russia accelerated its shift towards exporting LNG, particularly to Asian markets.
According to its Energy Strategy to 2050, Russia aims to increase its total LNG capacity to approximately 90-100 million tons per year by 2030.
Despite the potential for large supply sources, achieving this goal is proving difficult due to sanctions from the United States and the European Union.
Thus, the Ministry of Industry and Trade's assessment shows that Vietnam has the potential to access many international LNG sources, but each market has certain limitations. Qatar has the advantage of production scale, Australia and Malaysia have favorable transportation conditions, while supply from Russia is affected by sanctions.
Diversifying import markets, developing receiving infrastructure, and signing long-term supply contracts are therefore factors that need to be considered to ensure fuel supply for electricity production.

articles.full_text:
At least five people have been killed in Gaza and more than a dozen have been wounded in Israeli ground and air attacks.
Four Palestinians, including a young girl, were killed on Monday in an Israeli air attack on a camp for displaced people in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip, according to medical sources and first responders.
Another person was killed and others were wounded on Monday in an Israeli drone attack on the Remal neighbourhood, west of Gaza City, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Al-Shifa Hospital said the man was killed when the drone struck a group of displaced people in a tent.
Palestinian Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal said earlier on Monday that a total of 11 people had been killed and 50 wounded by Israeli fire and air strikes in Gaza over the past 24 hours.
“We transported three martyrs, including a child, following an Israeli air strike targeting a camp for displaced people in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis,” Basal told the AFP news agency.
Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis confirmed the three deaths, which have since risen to at least four, a source at the Gaza emergency services told Al Jazeera.
“Their bodies were torn apart by direct hits from shrapnel from the Israeli missile,” the hospital said, adding that several wounded people, including a child and a woman, had also come in for treatment.
The hospital identified three of the deceased as Hossam al-Zamli, 21, Tamer Abu Sneima, 24, and Jouri al-Soufi, who was only seven years old, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Education.
Israeli forces also set fire to a camp for displaced people at the Shujayea junction on Sunday night, forcibly displacing more than 200 families, or over 800 people, most of them women, children, elderly people and patients.
Gaza’s Ministry of Public Works and Housing said Israeli quadcopter drones set the camp ablaze at about 8pm, with fires consuming tents and belongings for several hours, continuing past midnight.
The ministry condemned the incident and called for urgent international aid to provide the displaced families with shelter and essential supplies.

ISLAMABAD - Federal Minister for Commerce Jam Kamal Khan and Qatar’s Minister of State for Foreign Trade Affairs Dr Ahmad bin Mohammed Al-Sayed co-chaired the second meeting of the Pakistan–Qatar Joint Task Force (JTF) on Trade and Investment in Doha and reviewed progress on bilateral economic cooperation and explore new opportunities for trade, investment and industrial partnerships.
Representatives of relevant Pakistani ministries participated virtually, while the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC), serving as the Secretariat of the Joint Task Force, coordinated the proceedings from Pakistan, said a news release issued here on Sunday. Both sides reviewed progress since the inaugural meeting in April 2026 and discussed measures to strengthen bilateral trade, facilitate investment and advance cooperation across priority economic sectors.
During the meeting, Pakistan emphasized the importance of the early signing of the Pakistan–Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Free Trade Agreement and sought Qatar’s continued support in expediting the remaining formalities. Pakistan informed the meeting that it had already completed its domestic approval process and forwarded the approved agreement text to the GCC Secretariat on December 31, 2025. The Pakistani side also raised the issue of restrictions on exports of bone-in meat to Qatar and requested their early resolution, highlighting that a comprehensive technical dossier addressing animal health and food safety requirements had already been shared with the relevant Qatari authorities.
In the agriculture and food security sector, Pakistan highlighted the proposed memorandum of understanding between the Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP) and Qatar’s Hassad Food for the supply of Pakistani rice under a government-to-government arrangement. The proposed agreement has been submitted to the Federal Cabinet for approval. Pakistan invited Qatari investment in modern agriculture, grain storage facilities, silos, cold storage, integrated cold-chain infrastructure and advanced farming technologies. Opportunities for developing sustainable food supply arrangements to strengthen food security in both countries were also discussed. Highlighting Pakistan’s industrial potential, the Pakistani side presented investment opportunities in the automobile sector, particularly New Energy Vehicles (NEVs) and electric vehicles under the country’s new EV policy framework. Possibilities for joint manufacturing, technology transfer and industrial partnerships were also highlighted.
Pakistan further invited Qatari investment in information technology and digital infrastructure, highlighting its growing IT exports and opportunities for technology partnerships and expansion of digital services. In the maritime sector, Pakistan identified opportunities for cooperation in shipping and maritime transport, particularly in securing oil tankers, LNG carriers and container vessels to strengthen energy security and international trade connectivity. The proposed new Karachi–Hyderabad Motorway was also presented as a potential investment opportunity for Qatar. The project would improve connectivity between Pakistani seaports and the national road network while facilitating regional transit trade, particularly with Central Asian countries.
The Qatari side emphasized enhanced cooperation in civil aviation and air traffic between the two countries.
Pakistan welcomed the proposal and informed the meeting that aviation-related matters would also be addressed through the Technical Working Group on Logistics and Communications.
The Pakistani side also presented the concept of an Investment Fund, highlighting opportunities for Qatari participation in infrastructure, agriculture, industrial development, information technology and other priority sectors.
During the discussions, Pakistan stressed the importance of early operationalization of the eleven Technical Working Groups identified during the first Joint Task Force meeting.
These groups cover priority sectors including logistics, aviation, advanced manufacturing, mining and minerals, agriculture, tourism, financial technology, healthcare, education, industrial development, information technology and startups.
Pakistan informed the meeting that it had already shared the composition of the eleven working groups and requested Qatar to communicate its corresponding nominations at the earliest to enable the groups to commence their work.
The Pakistani side further emphasized that the working groups should identify concrete trade and investment opportunities, address outstanding issues and prepare sector-wise progress reports and recommendations ahead of the Third Meeting of the Joint Task Force, to be hosted by Pakistan.
At the conclusion of the meeting, Federal Minister Jam Kamal Khan and Dr Ahmad bin Mohammed Al-Sayed formally signed the Minutes of the First Meeting of the Pakistan–Qatar Joint Task Force on Trade and Investment.

Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening bilateral economic cooperation through sustained engagement, improved trade facilitation, enhanced investment partnerships and effective follow-up under the Joint Task Force framework. Separately, Jam Kamal Khan held a bilateral meeting with Ms Nan Li Collins, Head of the World Investment Forum, in Doha, where both sides exchanged views on the ongoing regional situation and the challenges facing the global economic landscape. During the meeting, discussions focused on Pakistan’s constructive role in promoting regional cooperation and the importance of strengthening regional economic integration in the face of emerging global challenges. Both sides also exchanged views on the need for enhanced regional connectivity, closer economic cooperation and coordinated efforts to address shared challenges and promote greater regional integration.

articles.summary: Kazakhstan and UAE Advance Trans-Afghan Railway to Connect Central Asia With Pakistani Ports  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the United Arab Emirates have signed a strategic agreement to advance the Central Asia-South Asia (CASA) railway, an infrastructure corridor designed to link landlocked Eurasian markets with seaports in Pakistan. The proposed route through Afghanistan aims to handle up to 10 million tonnes of cargo annually, diversifying Central Asia's trade networks beyond the existing Middle Corridor and traditional Russian routes. The project reflects a broader geoeconomic shift as Central Asian republics actively seek independent maritime access.
The CASA railway agreement
The memorandum of cooperation, signed on September 30, 2026, by the transport ministries of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan alongside the UAE’s Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, formally initiates the technical and economic assessment of the trans-Afghan corridor. The project represents a fundamental shift in regional logistics, offering the landlocked republics a direct southern outlet to the Arabian Sea via the Pakistani ports of Karachi and Gwadar. The participating governments have committed to establishing a dedicated working group to evaluate the required railway infrastructure, outline logistics facility upgrades, and design viable financing mechanisms.
The strategic logic behind the CASA initiative is rooted in the urgent need for trade diversification. Historically reliant on northern routes through the Russian Federation, Central Asian exporters have increasingly sought alternative pathways to global markets amid geopolitical instability and sanctions regimes. While Kazakhstan has invested heavily in the Middle Corridor—a multimodal route traversing the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus to reach European markets—that pathway remains complex and subject to maritime bottlenecks. The southern route offers a continuous overland connection to the massive consumer markets of South Asia and direct access to the Indian Ocean maritime shipping lanes.
UAE’s logistical leverage
The inclusion of the United Arab Emirates as a primary partner brings crucial capital and operational expertise to a project that has struggled to move beyond the conceptual phase for years. Emirati logistics giants, such as AD Ports Group and DP World, possess extensive experience in integrating national railway networks with maritime terminals and dry ports. The UAE’s own Etihad Rail project provides a template for developing industrial clusters alongside transport corridors. By entering the Central Asian logistics sector at this early stage, the UAE is positioning itself to manage and profit from the future flow of agricultural commodities, critical minerals, and manufactured goods between Eurasia and the Gulf.
| CASA Railway Project Partners and Objectives |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Participating Nation | Primary Role | Strategic Objective | 
|---|---|---|
| Kazakhstan | Origin market and northern transit | Export diversification and access to Indian Ocean ports | 
| Uzbekistan | Regional transit hub | Integrating domestic rail networks with the Afghan border | 
| United Arab Emirates | Financing and technical logistics | Securing supply chains to Gulf markets and infrastructure revenue | 
| Pakistan | Maritime gateway | Increasing cargo throughput at Karachi and Gwadar terminals | 
Security risks and feasibility challenges
Despite the high-level political backing, the CASA railway faces formidable physical and security challenges. The route must traverse the difficult mountainous terrain of the Hindu Kush and operate securely within Afghanistan, a jurisdiction with severe infrastructure deficits and complex internal security dynamics. The estimated capacity of 10 million tonnes of annual cargo represents a theoretical projection of regional trade demand rather than a guaranteed immediate throughput. The ultimate viability of the corridor depends on aligning the transit tariffs, customs protocols, and border management procedures of four distinct national governments operating under vastly different regulatory frameworks.
The initiative has drawn significant attention from European powers seeking to secure stable supply chains for critical raw materials. Germany has expressed a distinct strategic interest in the development of Central Asian transport links. During a meeting in Astana on October 23, Kazakh Deputy Prime Minister Serik Zhumangarin and German Ambassador Heike Peitsch discussed the expansion of the southern route and its potential to bridge European and Asian markets. The bilateral dialogue, which followed President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s official visit to Germany, underscored that European economies view the diversification of Eurasian transport corridors as a necessary component of their own economic security.
The successful implementation of the CASA railway would cement Kazakhstan’s role as the primary logistics hub of the Eurasian landmass. By developing the southern corridor in tandem with its Caspian Sea infrastructure, the government in Astana aims to provide domestic exporters with the flexibility to pivot between European, Middle Eastern, and Asian markets based on prevailing economic conditions. However, the immediate task for the newly formed working group is to translate diplomatic memorandums into bankable engineering studies that can attract the billions of dollars required to lay track across one of the world's most challenging geopolitical landscapes.

Good morning, friends — we have a lot to celebrate today at EnterpriseHQ. EnterpriseAM Logistics is now EnterpriseAM Infrastructure. For three years, our Logistics edition has tracked how goods move through the region, from the Red Sea attacks that impacted Suez Canal traffic to the near-shutdown of Hormuz. We covered Syria’s overland corridors closing and reopening, Gulf ports absorbing redirected cargo, and what all of it cost the businesses caught in between.
Over the past few months, we’ve been asking a bigger question: what does someone who builds, finances, or depends on the region’s infrastructure need from us every morning? The Gulf is entering a decade of financing ports, pipelines, data centers, and industrial zones all at once, often off the same sovereign balance sheets. A port deal and a data-center deal are increasingly the same story: who’s paying, who controls the asset, and whether it holds up when it’s tested. Covering them in separate lanes means missing how the money and the control move together.
So we’re widening the lens across five categories. Commercial Infrastructure covers ports, free zones, rail, aviation, and the corridors that connect them. Energy Infrastructure looks at the pipelines, LNG, refineries, storage, and bunkering that keep the region running. Digital Infrastructure keeps an eye on data-center buildouts, fiber, the cloud, and satellites. Reserve Infrastructure covers stockpiles, food security, and backup networks — the infrastructure built to keep working when everything else doesn’t. And Social Infrastructure covers hospitals, schools, and housing, for what they demand of the systems around them. Whatever the category, every story we report answers three questions. Who builds it, finances it, and makes money from it? Is it built to hold? And what else depends on it — the port a rail line feeds, the grid a data center draws on?
Each issue has been rebuilt around these pillars. Every morning, The Lede gives you our point of view on the single most important thing of the day, and What We’re Tracking follows the projects still in progress, with the next milestone worth watching on each. Every Thursday, The Pipeline — our running tracker of the region’s megaprojects, from announced to funded, awarded, and under construction — tells you what moved that week. And once a month, Opinion takes a story already making the rounds and says plainly where we think the framing is wrong. You’ll also find The Stress Test, The Chokepoint, and The Corridor, which we’ll explain as they earn their place.
Today’s Lede puts all of it into practice: Saudi Arabia’s biggest new gas field is being built for the Kingdom’s power plants, not for export, and the first thing Jafurah sends abroad will be crude.
I want to thank EnterpriseAM Infrastructure’s editor, Farah Rafik, for pouring her soul into this relaunch — it couldn’t have happened without her. Another huge thank-you to the wider team, Omar Gouda, Youssef Ibrahim, and Marwan Ahmed, for the reporting and the months of work put into this new edition. And to our readers who’ve opened us every morning since the Logistics days, we hope you enjoy the new Infrastructure and everything we have in store for you in the weeks and months to come.

articles.title: Donald Trump advisers press for Israeli unity government excluding Itamar Ben-Gvir, Bezalel Smotrich - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Donald Trump advisers press for Israeli unity government excluding Itamar Ben-Gvir, Bezalel Smotrich  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
Voices within US President Donald Trump's inner circle are advocating for the establishment of a broad and moderate Israeli unity government without National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, with some even floating the idea of a rotation agreement in which Benjamin Netanyahu would serve as prime minister first.
However, Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot and former prime minister Naftali Bennett remain opposed to serving under him, and American officials have yet to discuss the framework with them.
American billionaire Bill Ackman, a prominent supporter of Trump with close ties to his circle, publicly called on Sunday for the formation of a broad, moderate Israeli government that excludes Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.
In a social media post, Ackman argued that such a government would allow Israel to restore its international standing, expand the Abraham Accords, and improve relations with both major political parties in the United States.
Ackman, who heads the hedge fund Pershing Square, supported Trump in the presidential election and is considered an influential figure in US political and business circles. He criticized Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, stating that their presence harms Israel's global image and its ability to advance key diplomatic objectives. At the same time, he praised Netanyahu and his relationship with Trump. Ackman favors Netanyahu remaining in office, but with a different set of coalition partners.
Realizing Trump's Middle East ambitions requires a change in Israel's Knesset
Ackman is not the only figure in Trump's orbit holding this view. According to several sources, additional figures in Washington believe that over the remaining two years of the president's term, realizing his ambitious Middle East plans requires a change in the composition of Israel's government.
Foremost among these plans is the possibility of a historic normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia, a prospect difficult to envision advancing while Ben-Gvir and Smotrich sit at the cabinet table.
Several senior advisors to Trump believe an Israeli government without Netanyahu's far-right partners would make it significantly easier to advance the president's regional policy.
This comes amid existing friction between Washington and Jerusalem: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are reportedly frustrated by the pace at which Netanyahu is advancing Trump's plan for Gaza; Special Envoy Tom Barrick disagrees with Israel's strategy regarding Syria; and officials around Secretary of State Marco Rubio seek to strengthen the Lebanese government while expressing frustration over insufficient action regarding Jewish violence in Judea and Samaria.
These officials place high importance on the composition of Israel's next government, which could impact Trump's chances of achieving major diplomatic breakthroughs before his term ends. A deal with Saudi Arabia, for instance, requires difficult Israeli decisions on the Palestinian issue and other regional matters.
A government reliant on Ben-Gvir and Smotrich could struggle to make such choices, even if Netanyahu himself were willing to do so. However, replacing coalition partners alone does not guarantee a deal: Riyadh maintains its own political demands, including tangible progress on the Palestinian issue.
Trump's inner circles question viability of diplomacy with Netanyahu around
Some within Trump's circle even question whether a diplomatic breakthrough is achievable as long as Netanyahu serves as prime minister. Consequently, an idea has emerged within the president's team for a rotation-based unity government: Netanyahu would serve during the first year, after which another prime minister would replace him to lead negotiations with the Saudis before the conclusion of Trump's term.
Proponents of the idea believe this arrangement would maintain governance continuity in the first year while entrusting regional diplomatic efforts to a prime minister who is not dependent on Netanyahu's current partners. According to several Israeli and American sources, Netanyahu told Trump he wants to form a unity government and will work toward that goal after the election.
Israel's Ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter, also publicly said Netanyahu wants a broad government. Leiter said Netanyahu prefers a national unity government over continuing with the current coalition makeup.
He also addressed Ben-Gvir's future, saying Netanyahu made it clear he would not serve as national security minister again. The comments drew a sharp reaction from Otzma Yehudit, whose officials fear Netanyahu is paving the way for a coalition with Eisenkot at the expense of his current partners. For his part, Ben-Gvir called on Netanyahu to form a right-wing government rather than one with Eisenkot.
Although the idea originated in his inner circle, Trump has not formally endorsed the initiative. The president publicly backed Netanyahu on October 18, even as several advisors expressed reservations. Vice President JD Vance did not join the public endorsement.
Furthermore, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee explicitly denied allegations of an American effort to push a unity government, clarifying that the administration does not intervene in Israeli elections or dictate actions to the prime minister.
Meanwhile, the proposals discussed in Washington remain far removed from Israel's political reality. American officials have not conducted a deep feasibility check with leaders of the change bloc, and no substantive talks have taken place with Eisenkot or other senior figures in the opposition regarding the proposed framework. Electoral scenarios also present obstacles for the initiative.
If Netanyahu's bloc secures 61 mandates, he is expected to receive the mandate to form a government, but it remains doubtful whether Eisenkot or Bennett would agree to join. Additionally, ultra-Orthodox parties demand the passage of the conscription bill as a precondition for coalition talks. Conversely, if the right-wing bloc fails to secure a majority, Netanyahu may not get the first chance to form a government.
Even in the event of a victory for the right-wing bloc, Netanyahu could find himself in a trap: his natural partners will demand the fulfillment of previous commitments, primarily the ultra-Orthodox demands regarding military draft legislation.
Reaching out to Eisenkot and Bennett would require offering them a partnership in a government they have pledged not to join. Even within the right-wing bloc, few believe Eisenkot or Bennett would consent to such a move.

articles.title: Conflicts in the Middle East are shifting global LNG flows. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Conflicts in the Middle East are shifting global LNG flows.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
VTV.vn - The Middle East conflict has disrupted LNG supplies, forcing Qatar to seek gas from the US and prompting importing countries to diversify their sources of supply.
Qatar signs long-term LNG purchase contract with the US.
Qatar Energy, Qatar's national energy company, has signed an agreement to purchase 4 million tons of liquefied natural gas (LNG) annually from Cheniere Energy of the United States, with a term extending until 2054. Shipments are expected to begin in the early 2030s, sourced from Cheniere's two export facilities in Louisiana and Texas. This is a significant move, as Qatar, already one of the world's largest LNG suppliers, now has to supplement its gas supply from a direct competitor.
Qatar's difficulties stem from the March attack on the Ras Laffan liquefied natural gas complex. Two production lines were damaged, affecting approximately 17% of the country's LNG export capacity. According to Qatari officials, repairs could take around three years. Meanwhile, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted, making it difficult for Qatar to deliver liquefied natural gas to international customers.
The agreement with Cheniere does not mean Qatar is abandoning its position as a major producer. Instead, the country is expanding its supply portfolio and LNG trading operations to increase its ability to fulfill its commitments to customers.
However, the new contract cannot immediately compensate for the disrupted gas supply, as deliveries are only expected to begin in the early 2030s. The deal shows that even resource-rich nations must adjust their strategies when both production and transportation face risks.
US expands its LNG market share.
Conflicts in the Middle East are creating new opportunities for the U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG) industry, as supply disruptions in the Gulf region prompt parties to seek alternative partners. The recently signed long-term contract with Qatar demonstrates the growing role of the U.S. in the global energy market.
The US has risen to become the world's largest LNG exporter in less than a decade, thanks to expanding liquefaction capacity and building export port systems.
You may also like
Current geopolitical shifts further highlight the advantages of suppliers with access to multiple markets and expanded supply sources. According to US officials, the country is continuing to boost its export capacity to meet international demand.
James Danly, Deputy Secretary of Energy of the United States, stated: "Essentially, the United States wants to leverage its position as the world's largest producer of oil and natural gas to provide abundant energy to as many customers as possible."
The US also has an advantage in its ability to deliver gas to multiple markets via various shipping routes. When supplies from the Middle East are disrupted, importers have an added incentive to seek partners that can help reduce their dependence on a single region or shipping route.
However, the US cannot immediately compensate for the disrupted LNG supply. In the short term, supply remains dependent on production capacity, export infrastructure, and international shipping conditions.
For American businesses, the conflict presents an opportunity to expand market share. But to translate this immediate advantage into long-term growth, the country's LNG industry still needs to ensure export capacity and the ability to meet customer demand.
Countries are seeking alternative energy sources.
The LNG crisis in the Middle East demonstrates that abundant resources are not enough to guarantee energy security if production and transportation are disrupted. Current fluctuations are also forcing importing countries to reassess the risks of supply routes and long-term gas procurement strategies.
For LNG, finding a new alternative supplier only solves part of the problem. The gas must be liquefied, transported by specialized vessels, and delivered to a suitable receiving port system. If shipping routes are disrupted, even if the supply still exists, it may not reach where it is needed.
The Strait of Hormuz is a prime example. This route is crucial to the Gulf region's energy exports. Obstacles there highlight how transport risks can exacerbate shortages when supplies are disrupted.
You may also like
Yukio Kani, CEO of JERA Energy Group, Japan, said: "Global LNG buyers are increasingly focusing on diversifying their gas purchase portfolios. Customers who are overly dependent on Qatar need to consider expanding their supply sources. Each buyer needs to diversify their supply sources."
For importing countries, the crisis also necessitates a rebalancing of LNG procurement strategies. Over-reliance on the spot market can lead to significantly increased costs as supply tightens. Meanwhile, long-term contracts offer buyers greater control over their supply and limit price volatility, although a combination of supply options is still necessary to mitigate risk.
Diversifying supply sources cannot be achieved overnight. Long-term contracts, LNG receiving capacity, and access to multiple shipping routes all require significant time and investment.
However, these options can help importing countries reduce their dependence on a single source or method of gas procurement. Energy security, therefore, lies not only in having sufficient gas supplies, but also in the ability to deliver that gas to the right place, at the right time, and with greater stability.
A major gas exporting power now having to seek alternative sources of supply demonstrates that resource advantages can also be reversed. Conflict in the Middle East could reshape energy flows and trade relations for decades. This is also an example of how, for economies , risk management must be at the heart of development strategy. A competitively priced energy source today is only truly an advantage if it remains available to the economy even during the most difficult times.

India, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and several African countries have forged a strong dynamic with one another over several decades, both bilaterally—highlighted by announcements such as the India–UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA)[a] and the recently signed UAE CEPAs with African nations, including Kenya[b] and Mauritius[c]—and through cooperation within multilateral platforms including BRICS and the Group of Twenty (G20). Trilateral partnerships have emerged as increasingly valuable frameworks for South–South cooperation, supporting development objectives while strengthening relationships.[d] Compared to bilateral arrangements, they enable partners to pool a wider range of resources, expertise, and knowledge to support development outcomes. At the same time, they offer a more flexible and inclusive approach than larger multilateral frameworks.
The first steps towards three-way cooperation were taken in 2019, when India and the UAE signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on development cooperation in Africa.[1] The UAE has since become one of Africa’s most active foreign state investors, deploying more than US$110 billion between 2019 and 2023, including over US$70 billion in renewable energy and green infrastructure.[2] DP World, a UAE-origin logistics entity, launched the Bharat Africa Setu to provide Indian exporters access to 53 African countries through its extensive physical logistical corridors, under the guidance of the Government of India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry and Ministry of External Affairs.[3] This was in addition to value-added services such as export finance, packaging, logistics, and certification. The hosting of the third iteration of ‘The Africa Debate—UAE’ in 2026 and the anticipated return of the India–Africa Forum Summit after an additional 11-year hiatus—although now delayed due to the ongoing Ebola public health concerns in parts of Africa—further demonstrate the growing relationship between India, the UAE, and Africa.[4]
The cooperation channels among the three nations will only continue to expand as strategic interests intersect across different sectors. Clean energy particularly presents a strong potential area of engagement, given its growing importance to all three partners. Accordingly, this brief examines the priority areas of collaboration within an energy-centric India–Africa–UAE (IAU) trilateral, while also assessing the financial mechanisms needed to mobilise the required capital. Given the diversity of African countries and their varying comparative advantages, different sections will examine specific countries and their potential roles within the trilateral framework.
Clean energy cooperation would comprise three verticals: renewable energy, including green hydrogen; grid infrastructure and storage development; and critical minerals (CMs). These are areas in which the three partners share complementary interests and ambitions. The trilateral should be institutionalised through IAU working groups, governed by a ministerial council and joint secretariat, and adopt guiding principles that foster long-term partnerships, inclusive and cooperative development, and sustainable operations. Three divisions of working groups should be established, focusing on the verticals of cooperation to ensure streamlined implementation of initiatives and projects. Each working group would ideally have a model that blends formal institutions from the UAE, India, and respective African nations with network-based partnerships, including private, public, and local actors.[5]

| Component | Members | Function | 
| Ministerial Council | Ministers of energy and ministers of investment/finance | Strategic political coordination and senior-level decision-making. | 
| Joint Secretariat | Staffed by officials seconded by signatories | Programme coordination, implementation monitoring, and stakeholder engagement. | 
| Technical Working Groups | Public sector and private sector firms | Sector-specific working groups focused on renewable energy, grid infrastructure, battery development, and CMs, providing technical coordination, planning, and implementation. | 
Source: Author’s own.
Sector-specific objectives and measurable outcomes have been outlined to steer collaboration within the working group and ensure the delivery of tangible results.
The advancement of energy transition agendas is a priority across India, the UAE, and African countries. The Africa Renewable Energy Initiative (AREI) has set a target of 300 gigawatts (GW) of renewable energy capacity across the continent by 2030.[6] The UAE’s Energy Strategy 2050 aims to triple renewable energy capacity to 14 GW by 2030.[7] Similarly, sustainable and green growth, with emphasis on clean energy expansion, is one of the core pillars of India’s Viksit Bharat 2047 vision.[8]
Africa is a particularly promising region for renewable energy deployment, given its vast resource potential. The continent's solar energy potential is estimated at approximately 482,216 GW, while its wind energy potential exceeds 71,778 GW.[9] Countries such as South Africa, Egypt, and Morocco have made remarkable progress in scaling solar and wind energy.[10] Hydropower is also emerging as an increasingly prominent energy source, although only around 10 percent of Africa's technical hydropower potential has been utilised to date.[11]
Countries including Nigeria, Morocco, Ethiopia, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and Mozambique possess substantial hydropower resources and are advancing policy initiatives and project pipelines to support further development.[12] Figure 1 illustrates the primary hotspots across Africa for each respective renewable energy source. Based on the Africa Finance Corporation 2025 analysis, wind potential is concentrated across North African and Central African countries as well as the southernmost and easternmost countries.[13] Hydropower potential is prominent across the central and eastern regions.
Figure 1: Leading Proven Resource Centres for Hydropower, Solar, Wind, and Geothermal Energy in Africa
Source: Africa Finance Corporation.[14]
In terms of operational capacities, India and the UAE provide extensive expertise in scaling and infrastructure development through established entities—the Adani Group and Masdar, respectively. Additionally, the two nations have developed growing expertise in value creation across the clean energy supply chain. India now manufactures most of its solar panels domestically, although key upstream inputs—particularly polysilicon and wafers—remain largely imported from China.[15]
The UAE has also gained experience in local value creation through overseas investments. For example, the 500 MW wind project in Morocco, developed by ACWA Power, is expected to supply power to an electric vehicle (EV) battery gigafactory.[16] The learnings gained by both countries in building industrial capacity could prove valuable in partnerships with African countries by supporting local content development, industrial value addition, and reducing overreliance on imported technologies from China—all priorities across the continent.
Each African country would also present strengths that can be harnessed during project execution. For example, South Africa is leading renewable deployment across the continent, courtesy of the enabling regulatory ecosystem created by the Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (REIPPPP).[17]
Furthermore, India, the UAE, and African countries comprising the Africa Green Hydrogen Alliance—Egypt, Kenya, Mauritania, Morocco, Namibia, South Africa, Algeria, Angola, Djibouti, Ethiopia, and Nigeria—are positioning themselves as key players in the global green hydrogen economy, presenting an important area for IAU trilateral cooperation.[18]
India has accelerated its green hydrogen ambitions through the National Green Hydrogen Mission, with the Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition Scheme providing financial incentives to expand domestic electrolyser manufacturing.[19] Meanwhile, the UAE’s hydrogen strategy aims to position the country as a leading producer and exporter of both green and blue hydrogen by 2031. Egypt and Mauritania have also established relations with UAE developer Masdar for green hydrogen development, with a signed MoU for the development of two green hydrogen production facilities in Egypt[20] and a US$34 billion deal for a green hydrogen project in Mauritania.[21]
Given that the partners are working to build a hydrogen ecosystem focused on domestic and international exports, a clusters-and-corridors approach could help create an integrated system among the IAU countries.[22] Industrial clusters centred on sectors such as fertilisers, chemicals, steel, and refining can help build domestic hydrogen demand while export corridors connecting production centres to partner-country markets can support economies of scale and attract investment, given the presence of off-take agreements. To maximise impact, trilateral cooperation should prioritise technology transfer and co-investment mechanisms that reduce project risks and accelerate deployment.[23]

articles.title: US has ‘two very different sets of intelligence reports’: Trump rules out Sunday strikes on Iran - The Times of India
articles.summary: US has ‘two very different sets of intelligence reports’: Trump rules out Sunday strikes on Iran  The Times of IndiaIran in ‘Advanced Stages’ of Planning Attacks Against Americans, Officials Say  The New York TimesU.S. Evacuates Mideast Outposts After Suspected Iranian Plot to Target Americans  WSJTrump Says US Has Two Different Sets of Intelligence on Iran  Bloomberg.comScoop: U.S. intel memo warns of "advanced" Iranian plots to kill officials abroad&nbsp...
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday ruled out an immediate military strike against Iran, saying Washington had no plans to launch an attack that day, even as conflicting intelligence assessments and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts continued to shape the US approach to Tehran.
"Would I tell you that? But the answer is no. There will not be a strike," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Michigan, responding to a question about whether military action against Iran could take place as soon as Sunday.
"We have two very different sets of intelligence reports," Trump said, describing the incoming information as "very advanced."
The president maintained that Washington was doing "well with Iran," although an unnamed US official told Israeli news channel i24NEWS that Trump was prepared to "shift gears on Iran" and that military strikes no longer appeared to be "a question of if, but of when."
The remarks came after Trump presented Tehran with a stark choice between reaching a diplomatic agreement and facing further military action.
"Do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off? That's the only question," Trump told Fox News, framing the next phase of the conflict as a choice between negotiations and escalating military operations.
Despite ruling out a strike on Sunday, Trump has continued to signal that Washington could pursue further military action if negotiations fail to produce an agreement.
Trump claims US controls Strait of Hormuz
Trump also asserted that American forces had established maritime dominance over the Strait of Hormuz, a key global shipping route and a major point of contention in the conflict with Iran.
"Remember, we now control the Hormuz Strait. They get nothing. Yes, we get everything." He maintained that commercial activity through the chokepoint had exceeded pre-war levels and described the US Navy's enforcement of a blockade on Iranian ports and shipping as "unbelievable."
On Saturday, Trump had suggested that Washington could either launch fresh military strikes or secure a comprehensive agreement with Tehran. He questioned whether Iran would honour any commitments under a potential deal, while arguing that either outcome would amount to an American victory.
Control over the Strait of Hormuz remains a central point of friction in the conflict, which erupted in late February following joint US-Israeli strikes. The confrontation has continued despite a ceasefire and a memorandum aimed at securing a final peace agreement.
Trump signals Russia-Ukraine peace talks
Turning to the war in Eastern Europe, Trump indicated that high-level diplomatic engagements involving the United States, Russia and Ukraine could take place soon.
"We're going to be having some pretty soon, and I think they both want to make a deal," he said, expressing optimism about the prospects of negotiations between Moscow and Kyiv.
Trump did not provide further details about the proposed engagements or specify when the talks would take place.
On Brazil's presidential election, the US president refrained from endorsing either candidate, saying his administration was "watching" the race.
Trump links European unrest to immigration
Trump also criticised immigration policies in European countries, linking protests and unrest in France, Italy, Belgium and Spain to what he described as inadequate border enforcement.
Contrasting the situation in Europe with US border controls, he claimed that the United States had prevented unauthorised crossings over the preceding 18 months.
"I closed the border. You know that we've had zero infiltration," Trump said, asserting that "zero illegal aliens" had entered the country during that period. He also claimed that previous US administrations had allowed millions of people to enter illegally.
Referring to his conversations with French President Emmanuel Macron, Trump said he had previously warned the French leader about the consequences of immigration policies.
"'You are destroying France. You're letting people come in that hate your country.'" Trump said he had told Macron.
He also cited migrant arrivals in Spain as evidence of what he described as wider instability across Europe.
Trump accuses Taiwan of taking US chip industry
On semiconductor manufacturing and trade, Trump accused Taiwan of taking over the US chip industry through low-cost production, renewing his criticism of the island's position in the global semiconductor supply chain.
"They stole our chip business, all of it, 100%, because they made chips at a ridiculous price, and they just pushed them in," Trump said.
He argued that stronger executive leadership in Washington could have prevented broader tensions with China over trade and technology.
Trump's comments come amid continuing US efforts to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing and address Washington's strategic competition with Beijing.

Canada and its partners are set to gather in Luxembourg on Nov. 30 to officiate the signing of the agreement establishing the new Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), the country's top official said in a statement on Monday.
"In an increasingly uncertain and divided world, Canada is working to bring together like-minded partners to mobilize and deploy private capital in support of collective security by unlocking long-term financing, expanding defense industrial production, and building more resilient supply chains," Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said.
"That work is bringing Canada together with Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Türkiye, and Ukraine to establish the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), with membership open to other allies and close partners who share the Bank’s objective of enhancing defence, security, and resilience capabilities," he added.
He also informed that the bank will be headquartered in Canada and have a European hub in Luxembourg.
"This will be a major step towards creating a new multilateral institution with a broad mandate to strengthen the defense, security, and resilience capabilities of its members. The bank will help countries invest in their own defense capabilities and industrial capacity, while supporting collective priorities," Champagne said.

articles.title: US told Venezuela to allow Machado's return 'weeks ago'
articles.summary: The Trump administration told Venezuela's interim authorities "weeks and weeks ago" that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado needs to be allowed to return to the country ahead o...
articles.full_text:
The Trump administration told Venezuela's interim authorities "weeks and weeks ago" that opposition leader Maria Corina Machado needs to be allowed to return to the country ahead of potential elections next year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday.
Rubio told reporters in a call that the government of acting President Delcy Rodríguez replied to the U.S. by saying that Machado was free to enter the country. Machado returned to Venezuela over the weekend.
"Weeks and weeks ago, we spoke to the interim authorities and just said, 'Look, our expectation is that she’s a Venezuelan, she belongs in her country. That’s the country she’s from. She should be allowed to return. She should be allowed to return unperturbed,’” Rubio said.
He noted that the U.S. had not discouraged Machado from returning to Venezuela except immediately after devastating earthquakes in June. He said that was because the U.S. believed the priority should be in getting humanitarian and emergency relief into the country.
Rubio spoke after Venezuelan authorities and opposition figures agreed last week on a blueprint to reform the country’s electoral process in order for free and fair elections to take place at some point in 2027.
He said the Trump administration, which captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January military operation and brought him to the U.S. to face drug-trafficking charges, would be watching events closely and urging all sides to comply with the new process.
"Obviously, we need to use our leverage with the government for the interim authorities to ensure that the process is moving forward in a responsible way," Rubio said. "Our goal here is to have an election."
Machado had been in hiding in Venezuela for most of 2025 before making a clandestine escape that December to Norway, where she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. She later gave her medal to President Donald Trump.
She returned to Venezuela on Sunday, her first appearance since the U.S. deposed Maduro and replaced him with Rodriguez, who had been his vice president and has now exceeded the time she was authorized to serve, with no election yet scheduled.
Rubio said the U.S. goal is to help put in a place a sustainable election architecture that will give all parties confidence in the vote.
To get there, Rubio said Venezuela must stabilize its economy and rebuild its institutions, including its courts and electoral council, and provide an open space for political expression that will hinge on press freedom and access to all media outlets, including online platforms.

articles.summary: Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro said Monday that a Supreme Court justice had prohibited him from traveling abroad, a day after his election defeat and refusal to...
articles.full_text:
Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro said Monday that a Supreme Court justice had prohibited him from traveling abroad, a day after his election defeat and refusal to acknowledge the result.
"I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also banned from leaving the country," the right-wing senator said, denouncing "a clear attempt to intimidate me."
The right-wing senator received 48.2% of the vote compared to 51.8% for incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro, denounced "a clear attempt to intimidate me."
The senator is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering during the financing of a biopic about his father. He denies any wrongdoing.
The 45-year-old said the decision to seize his passport stems from a statement made by his brother, U.S.-based former lawmaker Eduardo Bolsonaro, that Flavio would have to leave Brazil if he lost the election.
"I never said that," the defeated candidate insisted in the Instagram video.
Bolsonaro reiterated that he would seek to annul the election, arguing that an extension of voting hours on Sunday favored Lula, despite having also requested the measure.
He also promised to lead the resistance to Lula's government, however.
"To withstand the chaos, I'm going to organize the opposition," Bolsonaro said.
At a news conference Sunday, Bolsonaro said he planned to request an annulment of the election following a chaotic extension of voting at the request of both candidates. However, it's unclear what legal avenue he would have to do that.
Early signs from Brazil's institutions and from leaders across the region, including conservative presidents who oppose Lula, suggest the results will be respected nationally and internationally.
Even with the vote extension, Lula's win was decisive. The soon-to-be 81-year-old incumbent won more than 64 million votes compared to just under 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.
President of Brazil's electoral authority, Kassio Nunes, who was appointed to the Supreme Court by ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, was among those who recognized Lula's victory Sunday.
"This is a really uphill battle for Flavio Bolsonaro. Important Brazilian power brokers are closing ranks behind Lula, sometimes begrudgingly," said Brian Winter, Brazil analyst and editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly.
"I sense that Brazilian power brokers that matter don't really want to go down the path of a truly contested election," he said.
The key to Lula's win was the additional 14.1 million voters who showed up for the second-round election, including those who voted for other candidates in the first round. Analysts say three-quarters of those votes went to Lula, handing him the victory. And notably, the first round set a record for the number of Brazilians who decided not to vote, while the second round had the least number of abstentions ever.

articles.summary: Libya's transport ministry announced on Monday that airspace restrictions ​issued by the U.N.'s International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) back in 2015 during the country's c...
articles.full_text:
Libya's transport ministry announced on Monday that airspace restrictions issued by the U.N.'s International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) back in 2015 during the country's civil war have now been lifted.
The ministry said the decision, which was formally issued on Oct. 23, was announced by ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar at the opening of a meeting of civil aviation officials from the Middle East in Doha.
"This measure comes as a result of the notable progress made and the confidence placed in the capabilities of the Libyan civil aviation sector in recent times," the Tripoli-based Ministry of Transport said in a statement on its verified Facebook page.
The ministry, in a separate statement, said the North African country has received requests for permits to transit Libyan airspace that it characterized as "unprecedented demand from international airlines."
"The total number of permits registered for the 2026-2027 winter season has surged to 61,968 flights per month, effective from this November," the ministry said, calling it a significant jump from an average of 2,000 transit flights per month during the 2025-2026 season.
"Such an increase will generate substantial financial revenues using Libyan airspace," it added.
Libya slid into chaos after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi in a NATO-backed uprising in 2011. Three years later, a civil war broke out between armed factions vying for power and divided the country between eastern and western administrations.
The war caused damage to up to 20 aircraft, including Airbus models, at Tripoli International Airport in 2014.
There are currently few airlines operating flights in and out of Libya, and they have long been limited to destinations such as Tunisia, Jordan, Türkiye, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Sudan.
The ICAO's decision would be circulated to all 193 member states for their implementation, the ministry added.

articles.title: Russia reviewing proposals to ensure Black Sea grain shipping: Official
articles.summary: Russia is ​reviewing different proposals to ensure the ⁠safe ⁠transport of grain across the ​Black Sea ​and is ⁠also in contact with Türkiye on the matter, Russian Interfax news ag...
articles.full_text:
Russia is reviewing different proposals to ensure the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea and is also in contact with Türkiye on the matter, Russian Interfax news agency reported on Monday, citing Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov.
"We are in dialogue with all countries – and by that I mean Türkiye as well," the agency quoted Alimov as saying.
"And not just with Türkiye, we are discussing this issue with various countries," he also reportedly said, adding however, that so far, he did not see "any prospects for reviving the grain deal."
Türkiye, alongside the U.N. was credited with brokering the historic Black Sea Grain Initiative on July 22, 2022, in Istanbul to allow safe maritime passage for Ukrainian agricultural exports during the war with Russia.
However, Russia withdrew from the agreement in 2023, complaining that its own food and fertilizer exports faced serious obstacles.
Turkish officials have hinted earlier this year that Ankara was in contact with both Kyiv and Moscow regarding a plan for the safe passage of grain via the Black Sea.
Black Sea region has been recently a center of renewed tensions and attacks as part of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, with attacks also weighing on critical trade supplies, including oil and grain exports.
Interfax separately reported on Monday that African nations have recently become major buyers of Russian grain, primarily wheat.
