Algeria announced Monday plans to send troops to neighboring Niger at the request of authorities in Niamey, aiming to safeguard shared energy projects and economic interests between the two countries.
President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, who also serves as supreme commander of the armed forces and national defense minister, approved the deployment, the Algerian presidency said in a statement.
The move aims to "ensure the protection of shared Algerian-Nigerien energy and economic interests," it added.
The presidency said the decision was taken in accordance with the Constitution, particularly Articles 30 and 91, following a request from Niger's authorities.
Both chambers of Algeria's parliament – the Council of the Nation and the People's National Assembly – unanimously approved the deployment during closed-door plenary sessions Sunday, Oct. 25, according to the statement.

articles.title: After Vucic defeat, focus shifts on how student-backed list will govern
articles.summary: Serbia ​entered a new political era on Monday after a student-backed movement unseated longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a historic landslide victory that triggered nationwide ce...
articles.full_text:
Serbia entered a new political era on Monday after a student-backed movement unseated longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in a historic landslide victory that triggered nationwide celebrations, although uncertainty remained over how the new leaders would actually govern.
Tens of thousands took to the streets of Belgrade and other cities and towns across Serbia after Vucic conceded defeat late on Sunday, capping two years of largely peaceful anti-government protests calling for the populist ruler to step down.
With almost 99% of votes counted, the students' candidates had secured a commanding 52.7% of the vote, according to the State Election Commission, versus 39.2% for Vucic's Serbia Progressive Party (SNS)-led alliance.
That gives the students 139 seats in the 250-seat parliament, leaving the SNS alliance with 97, and the remainder held by minority parties. The constitution allows up to 90 days for the creation of a government, once the parliament is convened after the announcement of final results by the state election commission.
"I thought it was unbelievable, I still do not believe it. It was too long, and (Vucic) was pressuring us for a long, long time," said university administrator Marijana Radovanovic Pajovic.
Vucic dominated Serbian politics as prime minister or president from 2014. But he was swept from power by a list of student-backed candidates born out of anti-corruption protests following the deaths of 16 people in the collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad.
The students' win marks a profound political shift in the country of some 6 million people and is reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary's Viktor Orban in April.
It may also offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up across Europe in recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.
While the students' candidates include university professors, actors and farmers, the movement is without a leader, a strategy employed during protests to avoid any smear attempts by the government.
Thus, it is unclear who will become prime minister and assume other key positions in order to enact the students' domestic agenda, which aims to root out graft and improve schooling, and manage the country's place on the international stage.
"This corruption that has entered into all pores of our lives...of course it will change, we are hoping we will slowly go into that direction of a normal community," said 60-year-old insurance worker Svetlana Karagkozidou.
Prominent figures include the head of the students' candidate list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic, former central bank governor Dejan Soskic and Radomir Sajcic, a professor at Belgrade University, who spoke on behalf of the students following their victory.
However, not everyone welcomed the change.
"Changing the country like that so suddenly and all at once, I don’t like it. I don’t even know who is standing behind, who those people are, who will be leading the country," said 60-year-old civil worker Senka Radakovic.
Meanwhile, supporters of the student movement set about cleaning up a park near the parliament building in Belgrade that had long been used as a camp by Vucic's supporters. They removed metal barricades and tents and cleaned stickers off children's play equipment.
"I think it is one of Belgrade's most beautiful parks, that they took from us for a year or a year-and-a-half, and this is the least we can do right now," said one of the cleaning volunteers, Filip Beselinovic.

articles.title: Norway responds after Trump's sharp wording over Nobel prize
articles.summary: Norway brushed aside sharp criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday, saying it has no involvement in deciding the winners of the Nobel Peace Prize, long coveted by the Am...
articles.full_text:
Norway brushed aside sharp criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday, saying it has no involvement in deciding the winners of the Nobel Peace Prize, long coveted by the American leader.
Trump attacked Norway during a campaign rally a day earlier, calling it a "s***house country," and said that Norwegian immigrants were not welcome in the United States because its Nobel Committee had not awarded him the Peace Prize.
"Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a s***house country, actually," he said during Sunday's speech.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize.
Judge and former U.N. rights chief Navi Pillay of South Africa was this year's recipient.
Trump has called the committee's choice "a disgraceful and embarrassing decision" and argued that the award should have gone to him.
Trump also said Sunday he would welcome immigrants from certain countries but not Norway "because I didn't get the Nobel Prize."
"So I don't want anybody from Norway," he said during the rally in the Michigan town of Port Huron ahead of crucial U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
There was no official indication of a new U.S. policy on Norwegian immigrants.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide responded to Trump's comments about the Nobel Prize on Monday, maintaining that the committee is independent.
"He knows very well that the Nobel Committee is independent. We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering, and that is still the case," he told national broadcaster NRK.
Trump came under fire in 2018, during his first term, after using similar vulgar expressions to refer to Haiti and certain African countries.

articles.title: Bulgaria presidential election goes into runoff amid low turnout
articles.summary: Bulgaria’s presidential election ended inconclusively Sunday, with a record-low turnout sending the race to a runoff, election officials said. With only 22% of the eligible voters...
articles.full_text:
Bulgaria’s presidential election ended inconclusively Sunday, with a record-low turnout sending the race to a runoff, election officials said.
With only 22% of the eligible voters showing up, observers attributed the low turnout to a general mistrust in politicians resulting in voter apathy, will pit two contrasting political visions against each other in a highly polarized contest on Nov. 1.
In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-Western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist president, Iliana Yotova, setting clear lines of division regarding the country’s future relationships with other nations.
Bulgarians voted against a backdrop of growing economic hardship and drone attacks on Black Sea shipping. The vote is the first major test for the Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party of Prime Minister Rumen Radev after its triumph in parliamentary elections in April.
Despite a record number of candidates, the race had been expected to be decided in a runoff between incumbent Yotova, backed by Radev’s party, and former caretaker Prime Minister Gyurov, who is backed by pro-Western opposition parties.
The campaign focused heavily on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the widening hostilities in the Black Sea, where recent drone attacks on commercial vessels off Bulgaria’s coast have heightened security concerns in the European Union and NATO member country.
The strikes have raised concerns over Russia’s intentions to escalate the conflict and prompted the government to ask Bulgaria's partners for assistance to strengthen its maritime security.
Candidates also sought to address public anxiety over rising energy prices and inflation, as many families, particularly in rural areas, struggle to make ends meet.
The election had been expected to go to a runoff as none of the 27 candidates was expected to win outright. Turnout must be above 50% of 6.6 million registered voters, and the winner needs a majority of votes.
Yotova, a 62-year-old journalist and former member of the European Parliament, is the country's incumbent president and a front-runner in the race.
She previously served as vice president under Radev, during his two terms as head of state. She took over the presidency in January 2026, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and is now seeking her own mandate.
She's running as an independent but also has the official backing of Progressive Bulgaria and the Socialist Party, where her career began.
If she wins, Yotova will become Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
Analysts expect her to continue Radev’s policy to keep Bulgaria on its European path but at the same time call for improved relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine.
Addressing supporters at a rally this week, Yotova said she "advocated for peace through negotiations, rather than force.”
Observers say that Yotova’s victory would keep the presidency in the hands of the ruling majority and such concentration of power could prevent institutions maintaining effective checks and balances on policy decisions.
Yotova's main challenger is economist Andrei Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the central bank and caretaker prime minister who led the country in the early months of 2026. He is supported by the pro-Western reformist opposition.
Gyurov, who has often expressed firm support for Ukraine, signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his premiership.
"I want Bulgaria to have a voice of its own in Europe. A reliable NATO ally that defends its interests through preparedness, strong diplomacy and a clear position," he told supporters this week.
Exit poll results show Yotova with 3% to 4% ahead of Gyurov.
Presidents in Bulgaria are elected directly for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. While the post is primarily ceremonial, the direct election gives the president greater political authority.
The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.

articles.title: Brazil’s Lula makes history to win 4th term but Bolsonaro yet to cede
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term Sunday, the electoral body announced, defying polls and regional anti-incumbent trends to halt a wave of ri...
articles.full_text:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term Sunday, the electoral body announced, defying polls and regional anti-incumbent trends to halt a wave of right-wing victories across Latin America.
His opponent, Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, refused to accept defeat and said he would ask for the result to be annulled because a Supreme Court justice's Sunday ruling extended voting by two hours.
Bolsonaro led the election's first round but lost in the runoff by more than 4 million votes, rattling Brazilian financial markets that had bet on his victory.
His refusal to concede defeat echoes his father's reaction after losing to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later sentenced by the Supreme Court to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup to remain in power.
The scale of Flavio Bolsonaro's loss to Lula (more than twice his father's losing margin) and the fact his campaign also asked for an extension because of rains in the conservative-leaning south make any annulment unlikely, analysts said.
Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at the risk consultancy RANE, said there could be right-wing protests in coming days, but "it is very improbable that it will lead to the reversal of the result."
Investors expect recent bets on a change of government to unwind in a volatile week ahead on financial markets. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil's Bovespa index plunged nearly 15% in Asia trade on news of Lula's victory, while the Brazilian real was set to fall sharply against the U.S. dollar.
The victory marks another comeback in his career for Lula, an icon of the global left and the most dominant force in Brazilian politics this century.
The 80-year-old was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption charges that were later overturned, paving the way for him to beat Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election.
"He is a statesman, a giant," leftist federal lawmaker Erika Hilton, who was with Lula in Sao Paulo during the vote count, told Reuters.
At times, Lula's reelection seemed like a long shot, as voters soured on him and his Workers' Party after years of corruption scandals and rising prices, while sweeping social changes left the former metalworker and union leader looking out of touch with an increasingly app-based economy and its growing ranks of informal workers.
Pollsters said better-than-expected turnout had powered Lula to victory. Leonardo Barreto, the co-founder of consultancy Think Policy, said voters had chosen Lula's familiar embrace over Bolsonaro's novelty.
"People today are choosing between change, with some apprehension and a known path, which guarantees certain rights," he said.
During the campaign, Lula pointed to a track record of falling poverty and inequality, while unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation hit record lows during his third term.
He warned Bolsonaro would cut welfare spending, backslide on social advances and hand over Brazil's sovereignty to U.S. President Donald Trump, whose State Department led a campaign to get the Bolsonaros back to power.
Lula's win deprives Trump of a major addition to what has been a growing bloc of friendly right-wing Latin American governments that have embraced Washington's agenda on security and migration.
There was no immediate comment from Trump or the U.S. State Department, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Latin American leaders were quick to offer their congratulations.
Celso Amorim, a former Lula foreign minister, told Reuters the leftist "would be very important for establishing a point of balance in Latin America. Lula is that balance."
Lula becomes the first candidate since Brazil's return to democracy in the 1980s to be elected after finishing second in the first round.
His campaign this year mixed the kind of pragmatism and populism that has shaped his career in national politics for half a century, rolling out a slew of reforms aimed at improving the lives of workers and poor Brazilians.
These gained steam with late-campaign pledges that ranged from free nationwide weekend public transport (a measure requiring formal submission to Congress) to a 15% increase in his trademark welfare program that is already being implemented.
Lula also championed a constitutional amendment that became Brazil's biggest labor reform in decades, passing with wide support in Congress.
Still, Lula's fourth term could be his most difficult yet, after Brazil elected its most conservative Congress since returning to democracy in the 1980s.
Combined, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party and allied parties could control more than 280 seats in the Lower House and up to 50 seats in the Senate, enough for comfortable opposition majorities in both chambers.
That may deepen recent trends of presidents ceding power to Congress on the budget, major legislation and key nominations.
Lula faces an economy that his government forecasts will grow just 2.3% next year, adding to fiscal concerns tied to high interest rates and public debt that has risen past 82% of GDP, the highest since the pandemic.
Goldman Sachs said it expects Lula to make modest progress at most to contain spending in a fourth term, as he stays committed to a state-led growth model.
Surging household debt also concerns economists. Trying to address the issue, Lula rolled out a provisional ban on online betting and unveiled a new debt relief program during the campaign.
The incoming right-wing Congress will try to pass structural reforms that favor businesses, experts say, prompting spending cuts that could trigger popular backlash.

articles.title: Serbian student-led movement ousts Vucic in major election upset
articles.summary: Serbian leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat Sunday in an election challenging his long-standing rule, losing to a student-led opposition movement that has protested his right-w...
articles.full_text:
Serbian leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat Sunday in an election challenging his long-standing rule, losing to a student-led opposition movement that has protested his right-wing government for two years.
It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years.
Almost immediately, crowds flooded the streets of the capital Belgrade and other Serbian cities in an outburst of euphoric celebration.
Belgrade resident Dragana Kovacevic was thrilled that "everyone greets with smiles." She said "we are all too happy, finally we are becoming one normal and free country."
Maja Stetic said she feels "fantastic." Vucic's ouster, she said, "means liberation for me, means a new future for us and our children."
High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country.
Serbia's 6.4 million voters were electing lawmakers to the 250-member Parliament. In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Students' List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105.
"It is now clear that we have lost and the Students' List has won," Vucic told supporters at his party's election night event, though he blamed Serbia's independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an "American deep state" for the loss.
Vucic said that his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Students' List, which he said took around 2.2 million.
Radomir Saicic, a Students' List candidate, said "tonight is not just about results."
"It is about people who believed and continued to fight," he said. "This is a victory over fear ... it is nobody's trophy, it is a citizens victory. But victory carries responsibility."
Supporters of the Students' List drove around Belgrade in cars, honking horns, singing, shouting and chanting: "Aleksandar is gone," referring to Vucic.
Crowds swiftly dismantled the fences and tents at a park in central Belgrade where Vucic's loyalists had been camping for over a year and gathered earlier Sunday. One tent was later set on fire in the now-abandoned camp.
A group of young people could be seen throwing rocks at a withdrawing column of police cars and anti-riot vehicles.
The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day.
Police in anti-riot gear had cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters. Special police vehicles could be seen near the pro-Vucic camp, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city.
Vucic was seeking become Serbia's prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign.
Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station.
Dijana Hrka, the mother of one of the victims, was in the crowd celebrating in Belgrade. Sobbing, Hrka told N1 television: "I have been waiting for this moment for two years."
"Now I expect that they will all be held accountable," she said.
Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia's voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties – the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media.
While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia's fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office.
The newly formed Students' List movement was shaped by university students but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists.
This approach was meant to counter Vucic's one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students' message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia's economy and restore its democracy.
The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians. Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas – Vucic's traditional strongholds.
The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orbán after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government. It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests.
Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70%, unseen in Serbia since 2000. During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the world. Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time.
Recent Serbian elections had been marred by irregularities and the EU was closely watching the conduct of Sunday's vote in a candidate nation for the bloc's membership.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated the student movement, saying "people of Serbia turned out in record numbers to shape their country's future."
"We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union," she said.
Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities Sunday such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying.
Both international and local election monitors had expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists.
Local elections earlier this year in 10 municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists. The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.
